en: Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
There was a sage named Kapila Gautama, the best among the upholders of dharma, who,
like Gautama Kākṣīvata, was exhausted by his ascetic penance.
He who, like Kāśyapa, constantly resorted to blazing asceticism, and like Kāśyapa, attained supreme perfection through its increase. (Saundarananda 1.2)
Among those who offered oblations, he was like Vasiṣṭha in milking the cow for his own sake;
among his disciples who were perfected through austerity, he was like Vasiṣṭha in milking the cow;
by virtue of his greatness, he became like a second Dīrghatapas. (Saundarananda 1.3)
And he who, through his wisdom, was like a third [son] of both Kāyā and Aṅgiras; (1.4)
On the auspicious side of that vast Himavat mountain,
there was a field and a sanctuary, which became a hermitage for ascetic practices.
With its beautiful groves of trees and thickets, and its lush, soft,
green meadows, it always appeared like a cloud due to the canopy of smoke from the sacrificial offerings.
With its soft, smooth, and sandy ground, pale with scattered filaments, the region appeared as if it were adorned with cosmetic unguents.
He stood like one possessed of kinsmen by means of the lakes, which were pure, reckoned as sacred fords (tīrtha), purifying, inspiring, and filled with lotuses.
With rows of forests on all sides filled with fully developed fruits and flowers,
the mountain shone and flourished like a man possessed of effective means.
Though crowded with ascetics contented with wild rice and fruits, self-composed, peaceful, and free from worldly desire, it seemed utterly empty, as if devoid of all inhabitants.
There, the sound of the sacrificial fires being offered, of the peacocks crying out,
and of the holy bathing sites during ablutions was heard.
There, the deer, sleeping upon the sacrificial altars of pure grass,
shone as if they were offerings made with *mādhavī* flowers and parched grain.
Even the small animals there moved about peacefully with the deer,
as if they had learned discipline from the ascetics who were a refuge for all.
Even though the possibility of non-rebirth was doubtful and the scriptures were contested,
those whose wealth is austerity performed penance there as if they were perceiving it directly.
In that place, the Brahman was measured by some, yet not measured by others;
Soma was measured at the proper time, and never was he measured at an improper time.
Indifferent toward their bodies, with minds fixed on their own dharma,
those ascetics performed austerities with great effort as if they were filled with joy;
there, the sages, striving with hearts intent upon heaven, practiced their penances.
Through their passion for austerity, they seemed to bring about the destruction of dharma itself.
Then certain princes of the Ikṣvāku lineage, desiring to dwell there, went to that hermitage, which was a seat of splendor and a field of asceticism.
With bodies like pillars of gold, lion-like chests, and mighty arms,
they were the worthy recipients of great renown, prosperity, and discipline.
For those of noble form are indeed worthy of one who is unworthy, the great-souled of one whose mind is fickle, and the wise of a younger brother who is devoid of wisdom. (Saundarananda 1.20)
They could not endure the royal splendor that had come to them through their mother's dowry;
yet, out of devotion to their father, those Kautsas became Gautamas. (Saundarananda 1.22)
Just as two brothers born of the same father became Rāma Gārgya and Vāsudeva Gautama respectively due to their separate acceptance of teachers, so it was here.
And because they made their dwelling concealed by śākra trees,
therefore those born of the lineage of Ikṣvāku are known on earth as Śākyas.
Gautama performed for them rites befitting his own lineage,
just as the sage Bhārgava did for the prince Sagara.
As Kaṇva was to the swift Bharata, son of Śakuntalā,
so was the wise Vālmīki to the two intelligent sons of Maithilī.
That forest, by means of that sage and those preeminent kṣatriyas,
simultaneously bore the splendor of both the Brahminical and the Kṣatriya orders— peaceful and well-guarded.
Then, taking a water jar and desiring their prosperity,
that sage flew up into the sky and spoke to those sons of the king.
"Follow me in due order, without overstepping that stream which falls from this jar of inexhaustible water onto the earth. (Saundarananda 1.29)
Then, having said "So be it," and having prostrated with their heads,
they all mounted their well-decorated chariots drawn by swift horses.
Then, followed by them as they stood upon their chariots, he, moving through the sky,
sprinkled water over the edge of that hermitage’s grounds.
Having drawn a checkerboard pattern as if with auspicious signs, the sage stood there and addressed these words to the sons of the king: *Saundarananda 1.32*
"In this place, encircled by a moat and marked with the sign of a rim,
you must build a city after I have departed for the triple heaven."
Then, at one time, when that sage had departed, those heroes roamed about, unrestrained by youth like elephants without a goad. (Saundarananda 1.34)
Wearing leather finger-guards bound upon their hands,
with bows held in their grasp and great quivers filled with arrows, they were clad in tightly fastened garments.
Seeking to test his skill among both serpents and wild beasts,
they imitated the god-striding prowess of the son of Duṣyanta as he dwelt in the forest.
Seeing that they had returned to their natural state like aged tiger cubs,
the ascetics abandoned that forest and took up residence in the Himalayas.
Then, seeing that hermitage site empty of them, those whose minds were desolate sighed as they gazed upon the empty hermitage site. (Saundarananda 1.38)
Then those men of meritorious deeds, having attained increased prosperity,
obtained there great treasures described by those who knew them.
Enough! You possess many various and abundant treasures, free from all enemies, for the attainment of the entirety of dharma, artha, and kāma. *Saundarananda* 1.40.
Then, because they had acquired that site and because of the transformation of their past karma,
those who knew the proper sites established a magnificent city upon that ground.
With moats as wide as rivers, clearly defined great highways,
and massive ramparts like mountains, it was like another city of the Giver of Boons (Śiva).
With its white palaces as its lovely face, its well-arranged market-stalls,
and encircled by rows of mansions, it was like the interior valley of the Himavat mountain.
There, the king caused the Brahmins— who were learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and established in the six duties—
to recite prayers for the sake of peace and prosperity.
In that land, by his own power, he caused the punishments for servants to be proclaimed in order to turn back those who had been incited by aggressors from that territory. (Saundarananda 1.45)
In that place, they stationed as attendants those who were endowed with integrity, possessed of modesty, far-sighted,
worthy, brave, skillful, and well-born.
He appointed them to various duties suited to their capacities, according to their individual endowments of intellect, speech, prowess, and other such qualities.
Crowded with men who were wealthy, composed, well-learned, and free from pride, it shone like Mount Mandara filled with Kinnaras.
There, with joyful minds and desiring to please the citizens,
they established glorious abodes of fame known as "Gardens."
And by his command, out of an excellence of consciousness, they dug lotus ponds with water of supreme and foremost quality in all directions.
They established delightful and magnificent assembly halls along the roads and in the groves, as well as wells on every side.
Crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, yet not confused nor disordered;
where the wealth of supplicants was never hidden, while his own wisdom and prowess remained concealed.
It was like a storehouse for riches, a receptacle for splendors,
an abode for sciences, and a meeting place for all prosperities.
He was a wish-granting tree for the virtuous, a refuge for those seeking shelter,
a home for those who had mastered the scriptures, and a hitching post for those adorned with eloquence.
With social gatherings, festivals, gifts, and ritual observances, those heroes of great prowess adorned that city, the abode of the world. (Saundarananda 1.55)
Because they did not impose any unjust tax upon anyone, they filled that city in a very short time. (Saundarananda 1.56)
And because they established that city on the site of the hermitage of that seer Kapila, it was therefore called Kapilavastu.
Just as the cities of Kakanda, Makanda, and Kuśāmba are heard of in connection with their hermitages, so too is that [city] of Kapila.
Those sons, resembling Indra in their qualities, attained that city through noble splendor rather than through pride;
and from this they constantly acquired the fragrance of fame, like the illustrious sons of Yayāti.
Even though the princes acted as its protectors, the kingdom did not shine while it was without a king,
just as the sky does not gleam when the moon has not risen, even though thousands of stars are shining.
He who was the eldest among those brothers by both age and virtues, a bull in vigor among bulls—
there his beloved elders consecrated him, as the Ādityas consecrated the thousand-eyed Indra in heaven.
Possessed of right conduct, discipline, policy, and ritual action, he was devoted to dharma and not to the suffering of the senses;
surrounded by his brothers, he protected the kingdom like Saṃkrandana, followed by the Maruts, protects heaven.
In the epic poem *Saundarananda*, the first canto, titled "The Description of Kapilavastu," begins:
Then, after some time, there arose by hereditary succession a king named Śuddhodana, whose actions were pure and who had conquered his senses. (Saundarananda 2.1)
He who did not cling to sensual pleasures, nor was he amazed by the attainment of prosperity;
he did not despise others for their success, nor did he feel distressed because of others.
He was powerful, endowed with courage, learned, and wise;
he was valiant, possessed of sound judgment, steadfast, and of pleasant countenance.
He was handsome yet not arrogant, skillful yet not lacking in straightforwardness; he was radiant yet patient, and an agent of deeds yet free from self-conceit.
Though assailed by enemies in battle and sought for refuge by friends,
he never turned his face away, owing both to his splendor and his very desire to give.
Desiring to follow the path of righteousness trodden by former kings,
he followed his ancestors in conduct, bearing the burden of sovereignty as if it were a sacred initiation.
Through his fair conduct and protection, the subjects lived happily and free from anxiety, as if resting upon the lap of a father. (Saundarananda 2.7)
Whether he had mastered the scriptures or the arts of weaponry, or whether he was born into a noble family,
no one who came into his presence was seen to have failed in his purpose.
Though spoken to with words that were unpleasant yet beneficial, he listened without agitation;
having abandoned even much evil, he remembered even the slightest good deed. (Saundarananda 2.9)
He showed favor to those who bowed before him; he subdued the enemies of his lineage;
he protected those in distress; and he restrained those who did not abide on the path.
Generally, those who follow his conduct were seen acquiring virtues just as they acquired riches within that realm.
He studied the supreme Brahman and never wavered from his steadfastness;
through his gifts to worthy recipients, he committed no sin whatsoever. (Saundarananda 2.12)
With fortitude, he upheld his vow like a noble steed bearing its yoke;
for, fallen away from truth, he did not desire life even for a moment. (Saundarananda 2.13)
He attended upon the learned, shone forth through his self-possession, and gleamed before the disciplined like the moon in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. *Saundarananda* 2.14.
Through both his intellect and his study of the scriptures, he understood what was appropriate for this world and the next;
and through his fortitude and valor, he protected both his senses and his subjects. (Saundarananda 2.15)
He took away the suffering of the distressed and the exalted glory of his enemies; and by means of his policies, he acquired both the earth and even greater fame.
Being compassionate by nature, he was pained upon seeing those who were suffering;
yet, out of greed for fame, he did not offer sacrifices with wealth acquired through unjust means.
Because of his firm devotion and friendship toward his friends, even those who were devoid of merit,
he did not fail to give or to offer his own respective wealth out of his cheerful countenance.

He never ate the first portion of food without having offered it to the Arhats; he never failed to bathe; and he never milked a cow by unrighteous means out of a thirst for milk, as one might over-milk a cow for its own destruction.

He did not offer a tribute that had not been obtained, nor did he ascend to the pride of sovereignty; he sharpened his intellect through the scriptures for the sake of dharma, and not for the sake of fame.
Yet he did not afflict even those worthy of his affliction with unwholesome deeds;
and because of his noble nature, he did not fail to recognize the virtues even of his enemies.
Drawing the eyes of the people toward him with his physical form like the moon, he did not touch another's property on earth, as one would avoid a highly venomous serpent. (Saundarananda 2.22)
No one was harmed by him in his domain, nor was anyone wounded by anyone anywhere;
for he bestowed fearlessness upon the distressed with the bow held in his hand.
He looked upon even those who had committed offenses with a loving gaze, let alone those who had previously done him kindness; he refreshed them with gentle words.
He acquired many branches of knowledge, yet he felt no curiosity for sense-objects; he beheld the dharma of the Kṛta age, and even in times of hardship, he did not swerve from that dharma.
He constantly grew through virtues, he prospered through the excellence of his friends, he took refuge among the aged, and he did not turn toward the censurable path. (Saundarananda 2.26)
With his arrows he quelled his enemies; with his virtues he delighted his kinsmen;
through his [administrative] gaps he did not urge on his servants; and with his taxes he did not oppress his subjects. (Saundarananda 2.27)
Through protection and through valor, he caused the entire earth to flourish;
and by means of clear administration of justice, he caused the sacrificial sessions of the night to thrive.
By the conduct of a royal seer, he caused the fragrance of fame to grow within his lineage;
like the sun dispelling darkness with its radiance, he caused his enemies to be overwhelmed by his splendor.
He caused his ancestors to expand through the virtues of his noble sons,
and he nourished his subjects with his conduct, just as a rain cloud refreshes them with water.
Through his constant and vast acts of charity, he caused the Soma to flow for the Brahmins;
and by abiding in the duty of kingship, he caused the crops to ripen in due season.
He, who was free from hesitation, did not speak any discourse that was unrighteous;
and like a universal monarch, he led others toward righteousness for their upliftment.

He did not bestow any portion of the kingdom upon anyone other than Bali; rather, through his servants alone, he vigorously crushed the pride of his enemies. Furthermore, by means of his own virtues, he repeatedly elevated his lineage.
And he did not cause the subjects to suffer by means of the established order of all dharmas.
Unwearied, the sacrificer performed his rites at the proper time and caused the sacrificial ground to be measured out;
and through his protection, he caused the Brahmins to be measured out as free from agitation.
At the proper time, the gentle prince caused the Soma to be measured out according to the rules by his preceptors;
and by means of his ascetic power and splendor, he caused the army of his enemies to wither away.
The knower of the supreme dharma caused his subjects to dwell in the subtle dharma;
and by the very manifestation of dharma, he caused them to dwell in heaven at the proper time.
Even when clearly manifest, he did not allow one who was unrighteous to remain in positions of responsibility during times of hardship;
nor, out of mere affection or passion, did he promote one who was incompetent.
With his splendor and brilliance, he overawed his arrogant enemies;
and with his blazing lamp of fame, he illuminated the entire earth.
Out of compassion, and not for the sake of fame, he gave to the seeker;
and even after relinquishing great wealth, he incurred no infamy whatsoever.
Therefore, even when his enemy was afflicted by suffering, he did not abandon one who had come for refuge;
nor did he feel pride upon conquering even his arrogant foes.
He did not transgress the bounds of propriety out of desire, hatred, or even fear;
therefore, despite the presence of enjoyments, he did not indulge in the wandering of the senses.
By him no difficult task whatsoever was ever seen as impossible;
nor did he fail in his duty toward those who were either unpleasant or dear.
Accordingly, he drank the Soma and attained glory as prescribed by the ritual;
he constantly recited the Veda and practiced the dharma declared in the Veda.
Thus, by such qualities that were difficult to find,
that Śākya king— whose vassals were both impossible and possible to subdue— became like Śakra himself.
Then, at that time, the gods, desiring the Dharma,
wandered through the quarters of the world, wishing to behold the practice of righteousness.
As those righteous souls wandered the world in their desire to understand dharma,
they beheld that king, who was preeminently a soul of dharma.
Then, departing from the Tuṣita gods for the earth, the Bodhisattva made his vow for rebirth in the family of that lord of the earth.
At that time, that god among men had a queen named Māyā;
she was free from anger, darkness, and illusion, like the goddess Māyā herself in heaven.
Then, at that time, she saw in a dream an elephant with six tusks, white as Airāvata, entering her womb with majestic power. (Saundarananda 2.50)
Having heard that dream, the twice-born experts in dreams foretold the birth of that prince, who was destined to uphold prosperity, righteousness, and fame.
When that distinguished being was born— one who sought the destruction of birth—
the earth, though immovable, trembled like a ship struck by waves.
An unblemished rain of flowers fell from the sky by the rays of the sun,
as if shaken from the Caitraratha grove by the trunks of the elephants of the quarters.
In the sky, the drums resounded like those of the sporting Maruts;
the sun shone with exceeding brilliance, and an auspicious wind blew. (Saundarananda 2.54)
The Tuṣita and Śuddhāvāsa deities were indeed filled with joy,
out of great reverence for the True Dharma and out of compassion for sentient beings.
The supreme one, the bringer of the banner of welfare, approached Yaśaḥketu;
he shone with peaceful splendor like Dharma incarnate.
To the younger queen, Araṇyā, a son named Nanda was born, who brought constant joy to the family, like fire in the forest. (Saundarananda 2.57)
Long-armed, broad-chested, with shoulders like a lion’s and eyes like a bull’s, he who indeed bore the epithet "Sundara" (the Beautiful) because of his preeminent physique. (Saundarananda 2.58)
Like the month of Madhu arrived, like the moon risen in the sky,
and like the bodiless god of love endowed with a body, he shone with lovely splendor.
The lord of men, with supreme joy, raised them both up,
just as great wealth held in the hands of a virtuous person promotes both dharma and kama.
In time, those two noble sons grew up for his welfare,
just as Dharma and Artha arise for the prosperity of a noble man who undertakes great endeavors.
Between those two virtuous sons, that King of the Śākyas shone resplendent,
like the Middle Country clearly situated between the Himavat and Pāripātra mountains.
Then, after those two sons of the king had been consecrated and had gradually mastered their learning,
Nanda took constant delight in sensual pleasures, but Sarvārthasiddha did not find pleasure in them.
Having beheld the aged, the afflicted, and the dead, and reflecting upon the world as ignorant, his heart was filled with distress;
possessed of compassion for others deep within his heart and desiring to utterly destroy the fear of birth and death on all sides, he found no delight in the objects of the senses.
Out of world-weariness, having set his mind upon non-rebirth,
he departed from the king’s palace at night— indifferent to the sleeping, beautiful women, intent on going to the forest like a swan leaving a lake whose lotuses have been crushed.
In the epic poem *Saundarananda*, the second canto, titled "The Description of the King," concludes here.

Then, having abandoned Kapilavastu—which was crowded with throngs of horses, elephants, and chariots, magnificent, secure, and beloved by its people—he departed for the forest with a resolute mind. (Saundarananda 3.1)
Seeing those sages engaged in various fires and ascetic penances, and relying on diverse vows,
yet wretched in their craving for sense objects, he turned away from such unstable austerity.
Then, having attended upon Arāḍa, who taught liberation, as well as Upaśamamati and Udraka,
he whose mind was intent on reality abandoned them as well, for he was skilled in discerning what is not the path.
Reflecting upon what might be supreme in the world, he examined various scriptures;
failing to reach a definitive conclusion, he practiced even more difficult austerities under another teacher.
Then, perceiving that this was not the path, he abandoned even that extensive austerity;
having understood the supreme object of meditation, he partook of excellent food for the sake of attaining the realization of immortality.
With golden, thick arms like a yoke, the gait of a bull, and long eyes,
he approached a *plakṣa* tree growing from the earth, desiring to know the supreme method of ascetic discipline.

Having sat there with a resolute mind and an immovable steadfastness like that of the king of mountains, he conquered the fierce army of Māra; then he awakened to the auspicious state, which is unassailable and imperishable.

And having understood that his task was accomplished, the gods, their minds set on immortality, attained incomparable joy; yet the assembly of Māra, though once delighted, became dejected and was thrown into turmoil.
The earth with its mountains trembled, and Śiva blew his fire-mouthed conch;
the drums of the gods resounded, and the cloudless sky rained down. (Saundarananda 3.9)
And having realized the supreme truth that is ageless, the Lord, out of compassion,
went to the city of Varanasi, surrounded by his retinue, in order to demonstrate the eternal immortality.

Then, for the welfare of the world, the Seer set in motion the Wheel of Dharma before the assembly— a wheel with truth as its hub, with resolve, intelligence, and concentration as its rim, and with discipline as its spokes.
"Thus is suffering; this is its causal creeper that sets it in motion;
this is peace; and this is the means"—this supreme tetrad is distinguished according to its specific divisions. (Saundarananda 3.12)
And having proclaimed the peerless, irreversible, and supreme [Dharma] with its three turnings and twelvefold analysis,
the Seer first instructed him who was of the Kauṇḍinya lineage.
For he crossed over that fathomless ocean of faults— with its waters of hypocrisy, its crocodiles of mental anguish,
and its surging waves of anger, pride, and fear— and he caused the world to cross over as well.

Having disciplined many people among the Kāśīs and the Gayas, as well as at Giri-vraja, that one of supreme compassion then went to his father’s city out of a desire to show favor to it. *Saundarananda* 3.15.
For Gautama, whose body was like the sun, arose and dispelled the darkness— just as the sun does— for the worldling who is of the nature of sense-objects and pursues many various paths.
Then, from that point, he beheld Kapilavastu, renowned for its most auspicious sites, with its exceedingly pure dwellings and its sacred groves, as if it were a forest due to his state of detachment.

For he had become one who possessed nothing, his mind restrained and himself the master of his own soul; how much less, then, could he have attachment for kinsmen, people of his own country, friends, or material things—all of which produce manifold fears? (Saundarananda 3.18)

He did not rejoice at being honored, nor did he fall into grief through contempt; firm in his resolve, he underwent no change of state toward either the sword or sandalwood, nor toward suffering and pleasure. (Saundarananda 3.19)
Then the king, having learned that his son had approached the Tathāgata,
set out quickly, followed by his horses and chariots, out of eager longing to see his son.
Having looked upon the Sugata, the Tathāgata, and the king who was despondent in his intent,
as well as the rest of the people with tearful faces, he indeed flew up into the sky to console them.
He strode across the heavens as if upon the earth; he sat down again after having stood;
with an unmoving mind he lay down; he became manifold again, and likewise he became one. (Saundarananda 3.22)
He moved upon the water as if upon the earth, and he entered the earth as if it were water;
like a cloud in the sky, he rained down again and again, and he blazed like the newly risen sun. (Saundarananda 3.23)
Simultaneously blazing like fire and discharging water like a cloud,
he shone with a luster resembling molten gold, like a thundercloud illuminated by the twilight.
Beholding him, who was like a banner risen up encircled by a network of gold and jewels,
the king attained incomparable joy, and the people bowed down with great respect.
Then, perceiving that the lord of men had been made a fit vessel by his perfection of supernatural power,
and that the city folk were likewise inclined toward him, the Guide proclaimed the Dharma and Vinaya.
Then the king first obtained the fruit of both immortality and the perfection of the Dharma; having attained incomparable virtue, he bowed to the sage as if to his own teacher. (Saundarananda 3.27)
Then many Śākya bulls, who were skillful, possessed serene minds, and were terrified by the suffering of birth and death, went forth like bulls fleeing from the fear of a forest fire.

But even those who did not abandon their homes out of regard for their children, fathers, and mothers, they too undertook the rules of discipline until death and, with disciplined minds, maintained them. (Saundarananda 3.29)
He did not harm even the smallest creature, though he lived by killing others for his livelihood;
how much more so, then, one of noble birth who possessed vast virtues and was always compassionate—what need is there to mention his service to the Sage?

Though his own wealth was meager and he could not endure the insults of others, he did not seize the riches of another; for he trembled at the prospect of taking another's fortune as if it were a venomous serpent.

Although he was endowed with wealth, though he was young, and though his senses were restless for objects of desire, he never approached other men's wives; for he regarded them as superior even to riches.

No one spoke an untruth, nor did anyone utter even the truth if it were unpleasant; no one spoke even a gentle word that was harmful, and though they spoke what was beneficial, they never said anything intended for backbiting. (Saundarananda 3.33)
He was never seduced by the mind nor did he ever covet the wealth of others;
reflecting upon sensual pleasure as unhappiness, that virtuous man dwelt there as if already satisfied.
The compassionate one did not even think of causing harm to another;
for there, indeed, he saw every person regarding one another as a mother, a father, a son, or a friend.

He attained the correct vision that the fruit of karma will certainly exist in the future, as well as in the present and the past; and he saw that the course of the world is likewise determined. (Saundarananda 3.36)
Thus, by means of these ten kinds of supreme and abundant wholesome deeds,
people dwelt there in that degenerate age, even though its virtues were diminished, by taking refuge in the Sage.
And yet, because of those qualities, no one there desired the happiness of rebirth;
having realized that existence is entirely inauspicious, everyone turned toward the destruction of becoming, not toward further birth.
Even householders, free from doubt and possessing supremely pure vision, entered the stream; for many indeed did so, while others brought about even the thinning of the dust of passion.

Even those who were here devoted to renunciation, discipline, and restraint, though they moved through various difficult circumstances and diverse conditions of fortune, did not stray from the path of the virtuous.
Moreover, there was no fear from themselves, nor from others, nor from non-existence, nor from fate;
and in that place, the people rejoiced in the qualities of great happiness and abundance, as in the Kṛta age under Manu.

Thus that city became joyful, free from disease, and devoid of calamity— resembling the cities of the Kurus, Raghus, and Purus— while the Great Sage, the teacher of fearlessness, dwelt there for the sake of auspiciousness, having transcended all passion.
But while the sage was preaching the Dharma there, and while his kinsmen remained indifferent toward that Dharma,
Nanda, staying within the palace, devoted solely to the business of passion, dallied in the company of his beloved.
For like a ruddy goose united with his beloved mate, he who was worthy of love did not think of Vaiśravaṇa, nor of Śakra, for the sake of that state; how much less, then, of dharma?

Because she was called by three names—Sundarī on account of her fortune and her beauty, Māninī on account of her steadfastness and her pride, and Bhāminī on account of her radiance and her honor. (Saundarananda 4.3)
With her laughter as her swans, her eyes as her bees, and her full breasts as her lofty lotus buds,
that woman-lotus shone once more through the sun of her joy, who had arisen from her own family.
With a form that was exceedingly captivating and with gestures corresponding to that form,
she was indeed Sundarī in the world of men at that time— the Nandā among women and the Nanda among men.
That goddess was like one who wanders in the Nandana grove, and Nanda was the bringer of joy to his family;
they appeared as if created by the Sustainer of Beings, having surpassed mortals yet not quite reached the gods.

If Nanda did not obtain that Sundarī, or if she of the arched brows did not serve him, that pair would surely not shine, being incomplete like the night and the moon deprived of one another. (Saundarananda 4.7)
Like the target for Love and Passion, like the nest for Joy and Ecstasy,
like the vessel for Rapture and Contentment, he took as his wife that pair who were blinded by intoxication.
With eyes intent on gazing at one another, with minds attached to each other’s speech,
and with the body-unguents removed by their mutual embrace— that couple captivated one another.
Both of them, impassioned by love and dwelling by a mountain torrent like a kinnarī and a kimpuruṣa,
played together and shone brilliantly, as if vying with each other’s splendor of form.
By increasing their mutual passion, that couple delighted one another;
and by amusing one another during intervals of fatigue, they joyfully intoxicated one another with playful grace.

Then, desiring to serve his beloved, he adorned her not for the sake of enhancing her beauty, for she was already adorned by her own natural form—the very ornament of all ornaments. (Saundarananda 4.12)
Then, placing a mirror in his hand, she said to her beloved, "Hold this before me while I apply my forehead mark"; and he held it for her. (Saundarananda 4.13)
Then, observing her husband’s beard, she too applied a cosmetic mark in that same manner;
and Nanda, having corrected the reflection in the mirror with the breath of his sighs, struck it down.
She laughed inwardly at her husband’s graceful gestures and his deceit;
and though she was indeed angry with him, she knit her brows in a frown across her forehead. (Saundarananda 4.15)
With his left hand, languid with intoxication, he cast a lotus from his ear onto his shoulder;
and with its petals like fingers, he pressed that very same flower against his face, whose eyes were half-closed.
Then, out of fear, the river bowed its head before the feet of his beloved— which were like lotuses, with toes illuminated by the luster of her nails and set off by the sound of her moving anklets.
Then, with his head adorned by the blossoming flowers he had released, the lover shone as he performed a service for his beloved,
like a *nāga* tree on a golden altar bent down by the weight of its flowers, shaken by the wind.
With her gaze fixed upon the necklace displaced by his breasts, she raised him up, pressing him with both arms;
and with her earrings tilted as she turned her head, she laughed aloud, asking, "How have you been made thus? (Saundarananda 4.19)
Then, repeatedly looking at her husband’s face as his hand rested upon the mirror,
she completed that decorative mark on her cheek, which was moist with the paste of *tamāla* leaves.
Her face, with its *mālatī* leaf-like tilaka, copper-red lower lip, and eyes as long as her curls,
shone like a lotus with its stalk submerged, its tips reddened by the rising sun, and bees alighting upon it, covered in moss.
Then Nanda, respectfully holding a mirror as a witness to his adornment,
with eyes squinting to inspect the decorative marks, gazed at the face of his beloved as she playfully flirted.
Beholding his beloved’s face— charming with its distinctive earrings like a lotus pressed by *kāraṇḍava* ducks— Nanda became once again a bringer of joy to his beloved.
Then, in that palace within the celestial mansion, just as Nanda was rejoicing in the Nandana grove,
the Tathāgata, at the time when it was proper to go for alms, entered his house for alms.
With his face cast down and devoid of affection, he remained in his brother's house just as if he were in the house of a stranger;
then, due to the negligence of the servants, he departed again without having received even alms.
One woman crushed fragrant unguents for the body, while another perfumed her garments;
likewise, one prepared the ritual for bathing, and others wove fragrant garlands.
In that house, as they performed their graceful duties suited to play while attending to their husbands, some young women did not perceive the Buddha; for such was the fixed intention of the Buddha.
But a certain woman standing there upon the roof of the palace, having fixed her gaze through the lattice of a window,
beheld the Sugata emerging like the radiant sun from the womb of a cloud.
Considering there the respect due to her husband and her own devotion toward the Arhat, she stood before Nanda, desiring to speak; and by his permission, she then related this.
I suspect that the Blessed One, our teacher, has entered our home for the sake of favoring these people;
yet, having received neither alms, nor speech, nor a seat, he departs again as if from an empty wilderness.
Hearing that the great seer had entered his house and was departing again without receiving due honor, he—
adorned with variegated ornaments, garments, and garlands— trembled like a wish-fulfilling tree shaken by the wind.
Then, placing his lotus-like hands joined in reverence upon his head, he requested leave to depart from his beloved, saying:
"I shall go to pay my respects to my guru; you ought to grant me permission to do so."
Trembling, she embraced him like a creeper shaken by the wind;
with eyes wide and rolling from her sudden leap, she looked at him and, sighing deeply, spoke these words.
"I ought not to cause you, who are desirous of going to see your teacher, any hindrance to your dharma.
Go, noble son, and return very quickly, before this cosmetic paste has dried."
If you indeed become dilatory, I shall surely inflict a great punishment upon you;
I shall wake you repeatedly as you lie there with my two breasts pressed against you, yet I shall not speak to you.
Moreover, if you come to me while my body is still moist with un-dried ointments,
then I shall press you tightly with both my arms— arms that are now stripped of ornaments and still wet with unguents.
Thus addressed and pressed by her with a discordant voice, he said:
"I will do so; release me, O fierce one, before that teacher of mine has gone far away. (Saundarananda 4.37)
Then, released from her arms which were smeared with sandalwood paste from her breasts— yet not released by his mind—
he cast off his attire suited to love and assumed a form worthy of honor.

As her lover was departing, she brooded over him; with her eyes fixed motionless in vacant meditation, her ears pricked up, and her mouth agape like a doe that has seen a wandering deer, she stood there like a doe whose mouthful of grass has been cast away.
With his mind drawn away by the desire to see the sage, Nanda hastened toward his departure;
yet, casting backward glances, he proceeded slowly, looking back like an elephant gazing at its playful female calf.

Gazing with a sidelong glance at that beautiful woman, whose waist was slender and whose breasts and thighs were full—resembling a golden cleft in a mountain—Nanda was not satiated, as if he were drinking water with only one hand. (Saundarananda 4.41)
That reverence directed toward the Buddha drew him forward, while his love for his wife drew him back again;
due to this indecision, he neither went nor stayed, like a royal swan upon restless waves.
Having gone out of her sight, he quickly descended from the palace;
yet, upon hearing the sound of her anklets, he was seized once more by his heart and hung back.
Held back by his passion for sensual desire and drawn forward by his love for the Dharma,
he proceeded with difficulty, being turned back like a boat against the current of a river.

Then, on the road, he beheld the One Possessing the Ten Powers, who had cast off pride even in his father’s city and was free from the conceit of being a Tathāgata; he saw him moving slowly on all sides, like Indra’s ensign being honored as it follows behind a procession.
In the epic poem *Saundarananda*, the fourth canto, titled "The Request for His Wife," begins:

Then, having dismounted from their horses, chariots, and elephants, the Śākyas, having assumed appropriate attire according to their respective status, and the merchants from the great marketplaces, bowed out of devotion to the Great Sage. *Saundarananda* 5.1.
Some followed him for a moment after bowing; some, having bowed, departed according to their business;
others remained in their respective places, standing with palms joined, their eyes intent on gazing at him.

Then the Buddhas proceeded with difficulty along that royal road, which was like a great stream for the people full of devotion, just as a current flows during the onset of the rains into the channel of a river.
Then Nanda was unable to pay homage to the Tathāgata, who was being honored by great beings gathering on the road; yet he took delight in the majesty of his teacher.
Desiring to cast off his own attachment on the road, protecting the devotion of the people who held other views,
and wishing to win over Nanda who was headed toward home, the Sugata then took another path.
Then, being solitary-minded, he who knew the true path set out upon the solitary way;
having gone before him, he bowed down with a deep cry of reverence to that most excellent one, Nandīvimukta.

Turning slowly with reverence, his shoulders draped in his garment, his body bent forward, with his hands joined below his chest and his eyes cast upward, he spoke these words in a faltering voice: *Saundarananda 5.7*

Standing upon the palace roof, I heard that you had entered within for the sake of showing favor; therefore, I have come here in haste, without showing disrespect toward the great courtyards of your residence. (Saundarananda 5.8)
Therefore, O beloved of the virtuous, it would be well if you, O best of mendicants, would take your meal there for my sake;
for this sun, wishing to travel toward the meridian of the sky, seems to remind one of the time.
Thus addressed by him, who was prostrate with eyes upturned by affectionate pride,
the Sugata performed such a feat that he understood the purpose for which he had not partaken of food.
Then, having bowed to the sage, he set his mind on departing for home;
but the Sugata, whose eyes were like lotus petals, gave him his alms-bowl as a favor. (Saundarananda 5.11)

Then, for the sake of the fruit that comes from giving in this world, he, being self-restrained, took with his two lotus-like hands— capable of grasping a bow— the bowl of that peerless worthy recipient.

But Nanda, perceiving from afar that the Sugata was turning away with his mind elsewhere and his purpose accomplished, turned back even though he held the bowl in his hand; desiring to go home, he followed along the path while keeping his eyes upon the Sage.
When he, out of affection for his wife, was about to depart from home even while holding his alms-bowl,
the sage then bewildered him by obstructing the entrance to the street.
For the Sage perceived that Nanda possessed the seed of liberation, yet his knowledge was weak while the dust of the afflictions was intense;
since he was inclined toward the afflictions and characterized by sensual objects, the Sage drew him back.
The side of affliction is seen to be twofold, and likewise the side of purification is of two kinds:
that which has the self as its basis for one who emphasizes the power of causes, and that which has the external as its basis for one who values conditions.
But one who possesses superior power of the cause is liberated without effort, at the very moment of being struck;
whereas one whose intellect is led by conditions attains liberation through effort and by relying on another.
And Nanda, whose mind was led by external conviction, attained a state of identity with that which he relied upon;
for the Sage made such an effort in that regard because He desired to lift him out from the mire of affection.
But Nanda, writhing in grief, followed his teacher slowly and reluctantly,
brooding over the face of his wife, with its eyes restless in their gaze and its tilaka-mark still moist.
Then the Sage led him— whose arrival was marked by lovely garlands and necklaces due to the month of spring—
to a monastery that delighted the mind with the practice of knowledge, where the pleasures of women were shattered.
Then, seeing him so distressed, the Great Compassionate One felt compassion for a moment;
he touched his head with a hand marked by the wheel on its palm and spoke this to him: *Saundarananda 5.21*
O gentle one, as long as the destructive time has not arrived, apply your mind to tranquility;
for death strikes down everything with a total assault, regardless of the circumstances in which one finds oneself here.
Restrain the fickle mind from the unessential pleasures of desire, which are common to all and resemble a dream;
for there is no satisfaction for the world through desires, just as there is none for fire fanned by the wind through offerings.

The wealth of faith is the most excellent among all riches; the essence of wisdom is the greatest satisfaction among all tastes; the bliss of the inner self is the foremost among all pleasures; and delight in knowledge is the supreme among all delights, for it transcends suffering itself.

What is the best speaker of what is beneficial compared to well-wishers? What is weariness for the sake of Dharma compared to those with virtues? What is the supreme duty for the sake of knowledge compared to ritual acts? Why, then, having become a slave to the senses? (Saundarananda 5.25)
Therefore, choose that which is certain, free from fear, fatigue, and sorrow, independent of others, and unassailable by any;
choose that which is eternal, auspicious, and the bliss of peace—why endure misfortune for the sake of the objects of the senses?
There is no impurity for living beings equal to old age; there is no misfortune in the world equal to disease;
there is no fear on earth equal to death. Indeed, these three must be experienced by one who is powerless. (Saundarananda 5.27)
There is no snare equal to affection; there is no current as captivating as desire for grass;
likewise, there is no fire equal to the fire of passion. If these three do not exist, then you possess happiness.
The separation from loved ones is inevitable, and from that, sorrow is certain to be experienced;
other royal sages as well, having fallen into madness through sorrow, wandered about helplessly. (Saundarananda 5.29)
Therefore, don the armor made of wisdom; for the arrows of sorrow cannot strike one who is subdued by patience.
And kindle your own inner fire like a small spark to burn down the great thicket of existence.
Just as one who possesses knowledge and holds medicinal herbs in his hand cannot be bitten by any serpent,
so too one who is free from worldly expectations and has conquered the delusion of the world cannot be bitten by the serpent of sorrow.
Having established himself in yoga and having fully realized the truth, he does not experience terror at the time of death,
like a hero standing in battle, clad in armor, with a fine bow and mastery of weapons, desiring victory.
Thus addressed by the Tathāgata, who feels compassion for all beings,
Nanda, his voice faltering yet his heart sinking within, spoke "So be it" to the Sugata with boldness.

Then, wishing to rescue him from his negligence and perceiving that he was indeed a fit vessel for the sacred tradition, the Great Seer, with a mind full of loving-kindness, said: "Ānanda, ordain Nanda for the sake of peace. *Saundarananda 5.34*
Then the sage of Videha said to Nanda, who was weeping within his heart, "Come!
Thereupon Nanda approached him slowly and said, "I will not go forth into the religious life."
Having heard Nanda’s intention, the sage of Videha informed the Buddha;
and having learned his state of mind from him as well, the Great Sage spoke again to Nanda.
When I, his elder brother, had gone forth into homelessness, O unconquered one, and our brothers had likewise followed us into the religious life,
the Great Sage spoke again to Nanda concerning that state of mind regarding our kinsmen.
Those royal seers who, laughing, took refuge in the forests are surely not unknown to you;
desiring tranquility, they spat out their desires and were never thus attached to these wretched pleasures.
Having repeatedly observed the faults within households and having perceived the bliss resulting from their abandonment,
you are unable to leave this abode of Mithilā, just as one who is about to die cannot leave a land beset by calamities.
For one who is headed for the wilderness of saṃsāra, how can there be no desire to ascend the auspicious path—
like a merchant who has strayed from his caravan while being led back along that very same route?
He who, while his entire house is burning, lies down through delusion and does not flee from it,
would be a negligent man in a world ablaze with the fire of time, whose flames are disease and old age.
Just as a condemned man being led to his execution might laugh and chatter in his intoxication,
so too one who is being led toward death, heedless and with a perverted mind, is an object of pity while Death stands before him with noose in hand.

When kings and householders alike—having abandoned their wives and possessions—have gone, will go, and are indeed going away, how can there be any attachment to these impermanent dear ones? (Saundarananda 5.43)
I do not see anything in which pleasure does not turn into suffering through its transformation into something else;
therefore, attachment to anything is not appropriate, for if it were appropriate, there would be no sorrow when it passes away.

Therefore, gentle friend, having understood this world to be fickle, like an illusion, a painting, or a magician’s trick, and ending with what is called "dear ones"—if you have the resolve to cut through the snare of delusion, which is a snare of suffering, then abandon it. (Saundarananda 5.45)
Better is food that is unpleasant yet beneficial in its consequence than delicious food that is followed by harm;
for this reason, I urge you toward the auspicious and pure path, even though it is disagreeable.
Just as a nurse restrains a child and extracts a clod of earth that has entered his mouth,
so too, desiring to pull out the thorn of passion, I have indeed spoken harshly to you for your own benefit.
Just as a physician administers even an unpleasant medicine to a patient by restraining him,
so too have I spoken this which is contrary to your wishes, for it is beneficial in its ultimate result and intended as a favor.
Therefore, as long as this collection of conditions lasts and death has not yet arrived,
and as long as your age is capable of practicing yoga, apply your intellect to that which is most excellent.
Thus addressed by the compassionate Leader who desires his welfare, Nanda said:
"O Blessed One, I shall do all that you say; I will act exactly as you have commanded."
Then the sage of Videha took him up and led him away while he was still struggling;
with eyes overflowing with tears, he stripped away the beauty of the hair from that head which resembled a royal parasol.
Then his downcast face, wet with tears as his hair was being shaved off,
shone like a lotus in a pond whose stalks are bent and which is drenched by the rainwater.
Then Nanda, his garments dyed with the astringent decoction of tree-bark, overcome by anxiety like a newly captured lordly elephant,
appeared like the full moon at the end of the night when it has entered the dark fortnight and is sprinkled with the spray from a young elephant's trunk.
In the epic poem *Saundarananda*, this is the fifth canto, titled "The Renunciation of Nanda.

Then, with her husband led away by reverence, her affection led away, and her discontent created, Sundarī herself did not shine as she had while remaining right there upon the palace roof. *Saundarananda* 6.1.
Expecting her husband’s arrival, she leaned against the window with her breasts, facing the doorway;
with her earrings tilted askew on her face, she hung there with her girdle-string swaying.
With her ornaments disarrayed and her garments slipping,
Vinatā shone from that celestial chariot like the most excellent of Apsarases fallen from her vimāna at the exhaustion of her merit, gazing upon her beloved.
With her forehead perspiring from exhaustion, her cosmetic paste dried away by her sighs,
and her eyes restless with anxiety, she stood there with a face that betrayed her suspicion that her husband was elsewhere.
Then, from the exhaustion of remaining in that position for so long, she fell right there upon the couch;
she lay down sideways, her pearl necklace scattered, with one foot still lingering in its sandal.
Then, a certain woman there, unwilling to see her so sorrowful and tearful,
suddenly began to weep and made a loud noise with her feet upon the steps of the palace stairs.
Upon hearing the sound of footsteps on the stairs, she quickly sprang up again;
and suspecting the arrival of her beloved, she rejoiced with an intensity born of affection.
Terrifying the pigeons perched within the roof-ridges with the tinkling of her anklets,
she hurried down the interior of the staircase in her joy, without noticing that the hem of her silk garment had slipped off.
Having gazed upon that woman and being utterly deceived, she sighed again and returned to her bed;
with her face turned pale, she did not shine, like the sky at the onset of winter when the moon has lost its luster.

Distressed by the sight of her husband’s absence, burning with desire and anger, she sat down with her face resting in her hands and crossed the river of anxiety whose waters were made of grief. (Saundarananda 6.10)
Her face, a rival to the lotus, resting in her hand which was as copper-red as a young sprout,
shone like a lotus bent over a reflected lotus in the water.
Reflecting upon this through her feminine nature— even though her husband was present before her, full of affection and looking toward her— she,
finding no truth in him as he relied solely on religious duties, imagined various things and lamented in various ways.
"Thinking, 'I shall return to you while your face-paint is still fresh,' he made that promise to me.
For what reason, then, does he who was so fond of his promise now prove false to it, my beloved?"

How can this unprecedented transformation have come upon the noble, virtuous, and compassionate one— who is ever-fearing of me and exceedingly courteous— due to his own lack of affection or some fault of mine?
Surely the heart of my beloved, who delights in pleasure and follows my will, must be devoid of passion; for even if he still possessed desire, he would not have failed to come to protect my mind.
"Surely another woman, superior to me in beauty and disposition, was seen by my beloved;
for it was because he had thus employed deceptive conciliations that he departed, leaving me behind even as I clung to him. (Saundarananda 6.16)
The devotion he spoke of toward the Buddha was his instruction for approaching me;
for if he had possessed faith in the Sage, he would have feared untruth as he would a terrible death.

If, while wearing my mirror for the sake of its beauty, she should adorn herself with it while her mind is fixed on another man, and he too should wear it for the sake of another person—homage be to that man of fickle affection! (Saundarananda 6.18)
Those who do not wish to encounter such grief as this do not deserve to place their trust in men;
for where was his former devotion to me, and where is this abandonment of me in an instant, like that of an ordinary person?
Thus, having been separated from her beloved and suspecting something else regarding him, she spoke;
and that woman, having ascended the bewildered celestial chariot with tears in her eyes, addressed these words to her. (Saundarananda 6.20)

"Even though he is young, handsome, endowed with good fortune, and possessed of noble birth—yet he never once honored you as a lover; you are being overly anxious, for he will treat you otherwise. (Saundarananda 6.21)

Do not, out of malice, speak ill of your husband—that beloved, worthy of love, and doer of kindness—before your ladyship; for he knows no woman other than you, just as the ruddy goose knows no mate other than his own female partner.
Desiring to dwell at home for your sake and wishing to live for the purpose of pleasing you,
he was indeed ordained by his noble brother, the Tathāgata, with his face wet with tears.
Then, having heard that news concerning her husband, she suddenly sprang up with trembling limbs;
clasping her arms, she cried out loudly like a female elephant struck in the heart by a poisoned arrow.
With her gaze reddened by rising anger and her slender body trembling with anguish,
she fell down like a mango branch broken by the excessive weight of its fruit, her string of pearls shattered and disarrayed.
Wearing a garment of ruby-red hue, with a lotus-like face and eyes as broad as lotus petals, she— once like Lakṣmī herself—
now appeared like Lakṣmī fallen from her lotus, or like a lotus garland withered by the sun.
Reflecting again and again upon the virtues of her husband, she sighed deeply and grew weary;
she pressed her copper-colored forearms and fingertips against the armlet set with the splendor of jewels.
"Ornaments serve no purpose for me now," she said, and cast her jewelry in all directions;
fallen there without her ornaments, she shone like a creeper with its clusters of flowers scattered.
Thinking, "This was held by my beloved," she embraced the gold-handled mirror;
and with effort, she vigorously wiped her cheeks—upon which tamāla leaves had been applied—as if she were angry.
That female ruddy goose, her mate wounded by the tips of the hawk's wings, cried out piteously;
she seemed to vie with the pigeons perched upon the palace, whose throats were choked with cooing.
Though she lay upon a costly bed with limbs of golden hue, adorned with variegated soft coverings and inlaid with lapis lazuli and diamonds, she found no peace as she tossed about.
Beholding her husband’s ornaments, garments, and playful objects such as his lute, she entered into darkness; she cried out loudly and sank down as if she had fallen into a mire.
With her belly heaving from her sighs, Sundarī was like a cave in a mountain split open by a thunderbolt and fire;
burning within her heart with the fire of grief, she then became as if her mind were utterly distraught.
He wept, grew faint, cried out, languished, wandered, stood still, and lamented;
he brooded, became enraged, scattered his garlands, tore his face, and pulled at his garment. (Saundarananda 6.34)
Hearing that beautiful-toothed woman weeping so violently, the women were deeply distressed;
out of terror, they ascended from the inner apartments to the palace roof, like *kiṃnarīs* ascending the ridges of a mountain.
With their faces drenched and dejected by tears, like lotus ponds with their lotuses moistened by rain,
they lay down beside her according to their rank and as they pleased, burning with grief.
Surrounded by those women on the roof of the palace, that fair-limbed lady, emaciated by anxiety,
shone like a crescent moon in the midst of autumn enveloped by streaks of lightning.
Among them, she who was distinguished by her speech, worthy of respect, and senior in age, embraced her from behind, wiped away her tears, and spoke these words: *Saundarananda 6.38*
O queen of a royal seer, since your husband is devoted to dharma, grief is never appropriate for you;
for in the lineage of Ikṣvāku, the forest hermitages are the desired inheritance.
You likely know those women of the Śākya bulls who have set forth for liberation;
for them, whose vows of chastity are as firm as their reliance on desire, their very homes are like groves of asceticism.
If your husband has been stolen away by another woman because of her superior beauty and virtues, then shed your tears;
for what noble-minded, beautiful, and virtuous woman would not shed tears when her heart is wounded? (Saundarananda 6.41)
Moreover, even if some misfortune were to befall you, let there not be even a trace of tears here;
for there is no suffering greater than that which befalls a woman of noble birth who regards her husband as a deity.
But now, having been set free, you are at ease, healthy, established in the fruit, and seeing no misfortunes;
having cast off all longing and entered the Dharma, why do you weep in distress at a time for joy?
Although she was addressed in this way in many ways out of affection, she did not regain her composure at all;
then another woman spoke to her with love, words that were agreeable to her mind and appropriate for the occasion.
I speak the truth, for which I am firmly resolved: you shall soon behold your beloved once more.
Without you, he will remain there like a body devoid of consciousness, though it is the very refuge of living beings.
Even in the lap of Fortune he would not find peace if you were not there by his side;
even when dire calamities have arrived, he would feel no sorrow while beholding you.
Go to your peace and restrain your tears; protect your eyes from shedding these hot tears.
That affection for him which you have, and that passion, will find no delight in the Dharma once you are separated from him.
One might think here: "He will not cast off the saffron robe because he is of noble birth and a virtuous being.
But for one who has taken it up out of self-interest and is now facing toward the household life, what fault is there in relinquishing it again? (Saundarananda 6.48)
Thus, being consoled by her young companions, that beautiful woman, her heart stolen by her lover,
went toward the Draviḍa country like Rambhā in former times when she was surrounded by Apsarases as she headed for the earth.
The sixth canto, titled "The Lament for His Wife," in the epic poem *Saundarananda*.
Then Nanda, though bearing upon his body the emblem prescribed by the Teacher’s rule, did not do so with his heart;
distressed by thoughts directed toward his wife, he found no joy.

Established in his pleasure grove, he found no tranquility due to the floral splendor of the month of Puṣpa, the all-encompassing assault of the flower-bannered god, and the state of youth that makes one prone to wandering.
Standing dejected in the mango grove where bees were clinging and swooning, he of the arms long as a yoke yawned deeply; and having meditated upon his beloved, he drew her toward him like a bow.
Receiving the rain of delicate flowers from the mango trees like a pit of sawdust,
he sighed deeply after reflecting upon his wife, like a newly captured elephant confined in a pen.
He who removes the grief of those who seek refuge, yet causes grief to the arrogant,
took hold of his sorrowlessness and, becoming sorrowful, lamented for his beloved, who was like a grove of lovely *aśoka* trees.
Seeing Priyaṅgu, the beloved of his beloved, thin and fleeing as if in fear, he,
with tears in his eyes, remembered that dear one whose face was bathed in tears and who was as fair as the blossoms of the priyaṅgu tree.
Seeing a cuckoo perched upon the peak of a tilaka tree covered in blossoms,
he imagined it to be the white crest-lock of his beloved as she leaned against the watchtower draped in white silk.
Seeing a flowering *atimuktaka* creeper that had grown by embracing a mango tree, he then fell into this reflection: "The beautiful woman must have embraced me as well. (Saundarananda 7.8)

Even the *nāga* trees, though formidable with their clusters of blossoms, did not catch his eye there— like trees in a wilderness to one who is suffering— as they resembled ivory caskets filled with gold.

Though the spring season was present with its fragrant leaves, like Gandharva maidens filled with perfume, they did not captivate the nose of him whose mind was elsewhere and whose soul was full of grief; instead, they pierced his heart.
With cuckoos whose throats were reddened and peacocks with dark-blue necks, all contented and exceedingly joyful,
and with bees repeatedly licking the honey, the humming of that forest dispelled his mental distress.

There, burning within his heart with the fire of passion— whose fuel was his wife, whose smoke was discursive thought, and whose flame was darkness— he abandoned his fortitude and lamented various things.
Today I understand that what they have done, will do, and are doing is exceedingly difficult:
those who, having abandoned their beloved with tearful faces, have practiced, will practice, and are indeed practicing asceticism. (Saundarananda 7.13)
In this world, there is no bond as firm as this: neither one made of wood, nor of fiber, nor of iron;
rather, it is this very face, so mobile and charming speech.

For those fetters pass away only after being cut and broken through one's own manliness and the strength of friends; yet this bond consisting of affection cannot be released except through knowledge and harshness. (Saundarananda 7.15)
That knowledge which would lead to my peace does not exist in me, nor do I possess harshness, for I am compassionate by nature;
yet I am also possessed of desire, and the Buddha is my teacher—I stand between them like one caught in the path of a turning wheel.
For even though I have assumed the marks of a monk and have been twice instructed by my elder brother, the seer,
I find no peace in any state, like a cakravāka bird separated from its beloved.
Even now, that remains in my heart: how she, laughing mischievously, spoke to me when I had feigned anger at her in the mirror, saying, "O rogue, why have you done this? (Saundarananda 7.18)

The words she spoke to me with tearful eyes and a face of trembling gaze— saying, "While my face is still fresh and its makeup not yet faded"— those words of that young woman still weigh upon my heart even today.
Having assumed his posture while staying by a mountain waterfall, this monk meditates with composure;
surely he is not attached to anything like I am, for he sits thus, peaceful and as if satisfied.

Without heeding the song of the male cuckoos during the splendor of spring, and without even glancing about, this disciplined youth studies his scripture; I suspect that his mind is drawn away by his beloved.
Homage be to him, whose resolve is firm, whose curiosity and wonder have ceased;
to him who is peaceful in soul, whose mind is turned inward, and who wanders about free from longing.

Who, being in the prime of youth, could possess fortitude while gazing upon the water with its lotuses and the forest in full bloom, frequented by cuckoos, during the month of Madhu which acts as the enemy of dharma?

By their demeanor, pride, gait, grace, smiles, anger, intoxication, and speech, women captivated the hosts of gods, kings, and sages; why indeed would they not have cast us, such as we are, into confusion?
For Hiraṇyaretas, overcome by desire, consorted with Svāhā; and Maghavan, with Ahalyā. Deprived of such strength and resolve, I am a mere man conquered by women—how much more so! (Saundarananda 7.25)
We have heard that Sūrya, having conceived passion for Saraṇyū, fashioned [the chariot] for her pleasure;
having approached the mare who had become a horse, he begot from her those two who became the Aśvins. (Saundarananda 7.26)

On account of a woman, a battle lasted for many years between Vaivasvata and Agni, whose minds were obsessed with enmity and whose self-control and fortitude had faltered; who else here would not be moved by the cause of a woman?
Out of desire, that most excellent sage, Viśvāmitra, sent Akṣamālā to a dog-cooker woman;
from her was born his son Kapiñjalāda, who, like Vivasvat, was a devourer of the earth and its waters.
Parāśara, whose arrows were curses, consorted with Kālī, who was born from the womb of a fish;
from her, his high-souled son Dvaipāyana was begotten, the divider of the Vedas. (Saundarananda 7.29)
And Dvaipāyana, devoted to dharma, took his pleasure with a courtesan among the Kāśis,
by whose foot— adorned with trembling anklets— he was struck, like a cloud by a flash of lightning.
Likewise, Aṅgiras, the son of Brahmā, his mind overwhelmed by passion, served Sarasvatī;
there her son Sārasvata was born, who became the restorer of the lost Veda. (Saundarananda 7.31)
Likewise, at the sacrifice of the royal seer Dilīpa, Kāśyapa stood waiting for a celestial woman;
taking up the sacrificial ladle, he cast his own flowing luster into the fire, from which Asita was born.
Likewise, Aṅgada, having reached the limit of asceticism yet being overcome by desire, went to the Yamunā;
there he begot Rahītara, who was exceedingly wise, upon a doe frequented by deer.
Having beheld the princess Śāntā, even though he was dwelling in a forest that was itself peaceful,
the sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga wavered from his fortitude, like a mountain with lofty peaks during an earthquake.
He who, indifferent to sensory objects, abandoned his kingdom to dwell in the forest for the sake of becoming a Brahman-sage—
that son of Gādhi, carried away by Ghṛtācī, perceived ten years and one day as a single day.
In the same way, Stūlaśiras, touched by the arrows of Kandarpa, fainted for the sake of Rambhā;
he, who out of lust and anger had been indifferent to her when she refused him, cursed her.
And when his beloved Pramadvarā had her life-force snatched away by a serpent, Ruru repeatedly slew snakes; yet he did not do so out of anger, but rather to protect his ascetic merit.
The grandson of the Moon, marked with the virtues of fame, the son of Budha, possessing the power of a celestial sage—
thus reflecting upon the Apsaras Urvaśī, the royal seer, the son of Iḍā, fell into madness.
On the summit of the mountain, Tāljaṅgha, being possessed by lust for Menakā,
was struck angrily with his foot by Viśvāvasu like a hintāla tree with a thunderbolt.
When that supreme woman had perished in the waters of the Gaṅgā, King Jahnu, his heart overwhelmed by passion,
blocked the Gaṅgā with his two arms, like Maināka, the lord of mountains.

And King Śāntanu, the lamp of his lineage and son of Pratīpa, though possessed of a glorious body, reeled from the separation from the Gaṅgā like a *sāla* tree whose roots have been uprooted by the waters of the Gaṅgā; he was no longer master of himself.
Grieving for that woman Urvaśī, who had been carried off by the son of Sunanda and was now in the possession of his enemy,
Somavarman— whose armor was his virtuous conduct— wandered about with his very armor shattered by the fever of his mind.
When his wife died, that King Bhīmaka, who was of terrible power upon the earth, followed her in death;
he was renowned as Senāka because of his army, like a god who had taken up a host as his own.
When her husband Śāntanu had gone to heaven, Janamejaya, desiring to seize Kālī, encountered his death at the hands of Bhīṣma; yet he did not relinquish his obsessive longing for her.
Pāṇḍu was surely cursed by Madana; under the power of desire, he fell under the sway of women.
Because of the curse of the great seer, he did not reflect upon death as he approached Mādrī, even though he served what should not be served.
Even such multitudes of gods, kings, and sages have fallen under the power of women through the force of desire;
being weak in both wisdom and essential strength, how much more so am I, overwhelmed with distress at not seeing my beloved?
Therefore, I shall go back home once more and fulfill my desire according to the prescribed rites.
For the outward mark [of renunciation] is not fitting for one whose mind is elsewhere, whose senses are unsteady, and who has fallen from the path of Dharma.
Placing an alms-bowl in his hand, having shaved his head, having cast aside pride, and having put on a discolored robe—
he for whom there is neither joy nor steadfastness, neither stability nor peace, exists and yet does not exist, like a flickering lamp.
He who has gone forth yet has not emerged from sensual passion, who wears the saffron robe but is not free from impurity;
who carries an alms-bowl but is not a vessel for virtues—even while bearing the outward signs, he is neither a householder nor a monk.

"Even my reflection that it is not right to abandon the signs of one who possesses [the marks of] spiritual lineage after having once accepted them—that too vanishes when I consider those heroic kings who, having left the forest of asceticism, returned to their homes. (Saundarananda 7.50)

For the lord of Śālva together with his son, as well as Ambarīṣa, Rāma, Andhra, and Antideva the son of Saṃkṛti—having cast off their bark garments, they again donned fine silken robes; and having cut off their matted locks, they wore crowns once more.
Therefore, as soon as my teacher has departed from here for the sake of alms, I shall likewise depart from here for home, casting off the saffron robe.
For one who bears the venerable emblem with a faltering mind and a defiled intellect—whose understanding is impaired—there can be no welfare in the next world, nor even in this world of the living.
In the epic poem *Saundarananda*, the seventh canto, titled "Nanda’s Lamentation," begins as follows:
Then, approaching Nanda—who had restless eyes and was intensely eager to return home—a certain ascetic addressed him with a benevolent gaze and words of loving-kindness. (Saundarananda 8.1)
What is this face, clouded with tears, that reveals the darkness dwelling within your heart?
Take courage and restrain this agitation; for neither weeping nor tranquility is becoming in you.
Feeling arises in two ways, certainly within the mind and within the body;
those skilled in learning, ritual injunctions, and medical treatment are likewise of two kinds for these two.
Therefore, if this bodily ailment exists, let it be told quickly and fully to the physician;
for by concealing his disease, the patient soon encounters intense misfortune.
Now, tell me of this mental suffering; I shall declare the remedy for it here.
For those who know the inner self and are investigators are the physicians for a mind possessed by passion and darkness. (Saundarananda 8.5)
O gentle one, if you think it should be told to me, let the truth be spoken in its entirety;
for the ways of minds are manifold, filled with many secrets and agitated by passion.
Thus urged by him, he who wished to declare his own resolve then took hold of him by the hand with his own hand, desiring to speak of his intention.
Then, in that pure bower of creepers blooming with flowers, the two sat down;
they were as if embraced by the tender sprouts, which were moved by gentle breezes.
Then he spoke his desire, held within by heavy sighs—
words difficult for a learned man who has gone forth to speak even to a monk whose speech is refined by sacred learning.

If it were consistent with one who constantly practices the Dharma and maintains a mind of loving-kindness toward all living beings— that you, being compassionate by nature and virtuous, should show such a desire for my welfare while I am lacking in self-control.
For this very reason, I have a particular desire to speak with you, who are a speaker of what is fitting;
for I would not reveal this state of mind even to an unvirtuous person, were he to speak with a fickle nature.

Listen therefore to this from me in brief: I find no delight in the practice of dharma without my beloved, just as a *kiṃnara* of restrained seed finds no joy while wandering upon mountain peaks without his lover. (Saundarananda 8.12)

Averse to the happiness of dwelling in the forest, my desire is to go home by whatever means possible; for without her, I find no peace, like a king deprived of supreme sovereignty. (Saundarananda 8.13)
Then, having heard those words of him who was grieving while facing his beloved wife, that ascetic shook his head and spoke these words softly to himself: *Saundarananda 8.14*
Alas, how pitiable! The fickle deer, longing for his herd, has escaped from the great fear of the hunter, yet deceived by the sound of singing, he now seeks to enter the snare. (Saundarananda 8.15)
A bird indeed, once trapped in a net, was released by people desiring his welfare;
yet, while wandering through the forest rich in fruits and flowers, he sought to enter his cage of his own accord. (Saundarananda 8.16)
The young elephant, indeed, has been pulled out by his mother from the deep mud on the uneven riverbed;
yet, driven by thirst for water, he desires to cross back across that same crocodile-infested stream.
Sleeping in a shelter infested with snakes, the youth was awakened by another who had woken up; overcome by confusion, he sought to seize the fierce serpent himself.
Indeed, having flown up from a forest tree set ablaze by a great fire, the bird,
free from distress, desires once more to fall there out of longing for its nest.
Helpless indeed through the intoxication of passion, separated from his beloved due to fear of the hawk, the jīvajīvaka bird finds neither fortitude nor shame; he lives piteously.
Lacking self-mastery, possessed by thirst, and devoid of both compassion and wisdom, the wretched dog indeed desires to eat again the very food it has vomited itself. (Saundarananda 8.21)

Thus, having meditated upon him who was tormented by the grief of love and having gazed at him repeatedly, that ascetic, desiring his welfare, spoke these virtuous words that were unpleasant to hear. *Saundarananda 8.22*
If you do not investigate what is auspicious or inauspicious, but have your mind fixed solely upon sense-objects,
and if you have not attained the eye of wisdom, then no delight in the supreme good can truly belong to you.

For one whose mind is unattached, whose self is wavering, there is certainly no delight established in the Dharma—whether in hearing, grasping, retaining, understanding the ultimate truth, or in the tranquility of the mind. (Saundarananda 8.24)

But for one who perceives the defects in sense objects, who is fully contented, pure, and free from pride, whose mind is disciplined in the practices of tranquility, and whose intellect is perfected, there exists no lack of delight. (Saundarananda 8.25)
The thirsty man delights in the splendor of wealth; the fool delights in the pleasure of sensual desires;
but the virtuous man delights in tranquility, having transcended enjoyments through knowledge.

Moreover, the mind of one who is renowned, wise, of noble birth, and who honors the bearer of the [ascetic] marks, is not inclined toward the household life, just as the bending of a mountain cannot be caused by the force of the wind. *Saundarananda* 8.27.
He who, having despised his own independent sovereignty which rests within himself, would long for that which depends on others,
would be like one established on the auspicious path of tranquility longing for a home full of faults.

Just as one who has been released from prison might, when struck by misfortune, enter bondage once again, so too might one who has reached the forest seek out the bondage known as the household once more. *Saundarananda* 8.29.

And that man who, having abandoned strife, should desire to serve strife once more—he, a fool with uncontrolled senses, would abandon his [true] beloved and instead cherish one who has become like strife. (Saundarananda 8.30)
Like poisonous creepers that have been clung to, like caves infested with serpents that have been touched,
or like drawn swords that have been grasped— women indeed end in calamity.
Women who are intoxicated bestow intoxication, while women whose intoxication has vanished bring fear;
since they thus bring about both faults and fear, how indeed can they be worthy of being pursued?

Since kinsmen are divided by their own kin, and even friends by those who are friendly, it is the ignoble women who, being deceitful and intent on observing the faults of others, conduct themselves in such a manner. (Saundarananda 8.33)
That those born of noble lineage become wretched, that they engage in improper acts of violence,
and that they impetuously enter the front lines of battle— in all these matters, women are the cause.
They captivate with their lovely speech, yet they strike with a sharpened mind;
honey dwells in the words of women, but in their hearts is the great poison *hālāhala*.
Even a burning fire can be grasped; even the bodiless wind can be grasped;
even an enraged serpent can be grasped; but the mind of the wicked cannot be grasped.
They do not consider physical beauty, nor fortune, nor intellect, nor lineage, nor prowess;
women strike out without distinction, like rivers teeming with shoals of crocodiles.
A woman never remembers sweet words, nor endearments, nor even a true friend;
once she has been won, she is as fickle as a lightning flash, and thus she should not be relied upon here, just as one would not trust enemies.
