When they do not give, women become playful; when they give, they fall into confusion.
Toward those who bow before them, they become arrogant, yet toward those who are proud, they are most satisfied.
They behave toward those with virtues as toward a master; they behave toward those devoid of virtues as toward a son;
they behave toward the wealthy with longing, and toward the destitute with contempt. (Saundarananda 8.40)
Just as a cow, even when stolen, continues to graze as it moves from one pasture to another, so too does a woman, having gone elsewhere,
take her pleasure there without regard for her former affection.
For women indeed enter even the funeral pyre and even follow [their husbands] while still alive;
they may even endure physical restraints, yet they do not carry affection within their hearts.
Those women who, in some rare instance, delight their husbands by regarding them as deities, delight their own hearts by the thousands through the fickleness of their minds. (Saundarananda 8.43)
It is said that Senajit’s daughter desired a dog-cooker, and Kumudvatī, a fish-eater;
likewise, Bṛhadrathā desired a lion. Thus, there is no limit to the desires of women.

The descendants of Kuru, Haihaya, and Vṛṣṇi; Śambara, whose armor was composed of many illusions; and the sage Gautama of fierce austerities—all of them were overcome by passion stirred up by women. (Saundarananda 8.45)
The mind of women is thus ungrateful, ignoble, and unstable;
how could a wise man allow his heart to be attached to them, whose very nature is fickle? (Saundarananda 8.46)
O you of subtle intellect, do you not see that their hearts are both fragile and inauspicious? Why then do you not see that this body is a leaking house of falsehood, impure with excrement?

O you whose vision is shrouded by darkness, you perceive as beautiful that which is impure— the ointments, collyriums, garlands, gems, pearls, refined gold, and fine silks— which are daily adorned with grooming, garments, and ornaments; yet you do not realize this.
Or rather, you perceive that body as foul, yet you possess no true awareness;
for you perform fragrant rites for the sake of pacifying the impurity from which it originated.

Covered in the mud of impurity and naked, with their nails, teeth, and body hair in their natural state—if this is what is considered virtuous here, then let that which is innate in women be sought for purity among them. (Saundarananda 8.50)
If that Sundarī of yours were to become covered in the mire of impurity, naked, with her nails, teeth, and hair in their natural state, she would certainly no longer be beautiful to you today.
What man of discernment would touch a woman, who is like a leaking and filthy cracked pot, were she not covered by a skin as thin as a fly’s wing? (Saundarananda 8.52)
If you perceive the bodies of women as mere skeletons enveloped in skin,
yet you are still forcibly drawn by passion, O pitiless one, then you truly perceive the bodies of women.
Imagining beauty in what is impure— among nails, teeth, skin, hair, and body hair—
O lack of discernment, do you not see the true nature and the origin of women?
Having understood that both mind and body are especially full of faults,
let the fickle mind that yearns for worldly existence be restrained by the power of analytical reflection.
Being learned, wise, and of noble birth, you are a vessel for the highest tranquility;
having approached it, you ought not, under any circumstances, to violate the rule of restraint.
For one of noble birth, high-minded, fond of fame, and desiring great respect,
even death is better for a steadfast soul than life lived devoid of discipline.
For just as one who has donned armor and taken up his bow becomes blameworthy if he flees from the battlefield while standing in his chariot,
so too does one become blameworthy who, having adopted the outward signs of a mendicant, allows the horses of his senses to be carried away by desire.

Just as one who, though wearing supreme ornaments, garments, and garlands, wanders for alms bearing a bow and a shimmering, variegated crown, is an object of laughter; so too is one who has accepted deformity and subsists on the food of others, yet remains full of craving and intent upon the pleasures of the household—a source of ridicule.
Just as a boar that has eaten fine food and even lain down on a most excellent couch might, once released, run again toward its familiar filth;
so too, having heard what is beneficial and tasted the bliss of tranquility, one who is parched with desire for sense-pleasures might abandon the virtuous and peaceful forest and long for home.
Just as a torch held in the hand burns when its flame is fanned by the wind, just as a serpent, impetuous with rage, bites when stepped upon by the foot,
and just as even a tiger cub kills when seized while staying within the house, so too does association with women lead to various kinds of misfortune on this earth.
Having understood these faults inherent in women that are fixed upon the mind and body, and considering sensual pleasure to be as unstable as river water, leading only to affliction and grief;
and seeing the world to be weak like an unripe leaf, assailed by death—you should apply incomparable resolve toward liberation; you ought not to feel longing.
In the great poem *Saundarananda*, the eighth canto, titled "The Obstacle of Women":
Now, although he had been addressed in this manner by that monk, he did not at all attain tranquility regarding his beloved;
for, thinking only of her at that moment, he did not hear the words of the one who was like him in being unconscious [of them]. (Saundarananda 9.1)

Just as a dying patient does not accept the beneficial words of a physician who desires his well-being, even so he did not accept those beneficial words from me, despite my [advice] regarding strength, beauty, and youth. (Saundarananda 9.2)
And it is not surprising here if the mind, its intellect shrouded by darkness, should be overcome by the evil of passion;
for a man's evil ceases only when that darkness has reached its end and become thin. (Saundarananda 9.3)
Then, observing him thus cast down by his own strength, beauty, and youth,
yet remaining resolved upon departing for home, that ascetic instructed Nanda for the sake of his peace.
I understand strength, beauty, and fresh youth just as you understand them; yet, regarding these three things of yours which are unstable, you do not perceive them for what they truly are.
For this body is an abode of disease, subject to old age, and as unstable as a tree on a riverbank;
it is as frail as water-foam, yet you do not realize this, whereby you imagine yourself to be established in strength.

Since the body is seen to be on the verge of ruin through both the non-observance and the excessive observance of food, drink, seats, vehicles, and activities—for what reason do you still maintain pride in your strength? (Saundarananda 9.7)

When the world is afflicted by misfortunes such as cold, heat, disease, old age, hunger, and the like—just as water in the month of Śuci is diminished by the rays of the sun—why, O one proud of your strength, do you think it will not come to its end? (Saundarananda 9.8)

This body, consisting of skin, bone, flesh, and blood, persists only by virtue of food; it is perpetually afflicted and requires constant remedial action. How can you be deluded, thinking "I am endowed with strength"? (Saundarananda 9.9)

Just as a man might desire to cross the turbulent great ocean by relying on an unbaked clay jar, so too does one who exerts his strength for the sake of sense-objects persist in maintaining a worthless physical frame. (Saundarananda 9.10)

A man might wish to cross the turbulent great ocean by relying on a raw earthen vessel—even one that is unbaked—though it were to remain intact if held properly; yet in my view, this body is utterly devoid of substance. (Saundarananda 9.11)
When the elements of water, earth, air, and fire— always mutually opposed like venomous serpents—
are present within the body and lead to misfortune, how can you, O physician, determine the strength of a disease?
Serpents are brought to pacification by mantras, but the elements cannot be subdued by mantras;
serpents bite only here and there and only occasionally, whereas the elements always and everywhere cause affliction.

For this body, though long cared for with beds, seats, drinks, and food, and possessed of many qualities, does not tolerate even a single transgression, since it becomes enraged like a great venomous serpent. (Saundarananda 9.14)
When one afflicted by cold resorts to fire, or when struck by the heat of summer longs for snow;
when oppressed by hunger seeks food, or possessed by thirst seeks water—whence comes strength, what is it, how is it, and to whom does it belong? (Saundarananda 9.15)
Thus, knowing the body to be afflicted in this way, you ought not to think, "I am endowed with strength.
The world is without essence, without end, and uncertain; and in this impermanent world, strength is unstable.

Where is that strength of the thousand-armed Arjuna Kārtavīrya, who was so proud of his power, whose many arms Bhārgava lopped off in battle like a thunderbolt strikes the great peaks of a mountain? (Saundarananda 9.17)

Where is that strength of Hari, the drawer of Kaṃsa’s bow, who split the temples of the king of horses—that Jarā who, with a single arrow, struck him down as old age strikes down even the most excellent beauty in due course? (Saundarananda 9.18)

Where is that strength of Namuci—the son of Diti, who incited the wrath of the immortals and shone amidst his host—which Vāsava struck down with a mere fragment of foam while he stood in battle like the enraged God of Death? (Saundarananda 9.19)

Where had that strength of the Kurus gone at that time? Having blazed with speed and vigor in battle like sacrificial fires kindled with fuel, they now lie with their life-breaths extinguished, reduced to ashes.

Therefore, having understood that the strength of those who pride themselves on their power has been crushed, and reflecting upon how the world is subject to old age and death, you ought not to maintain pride regarding strength. (Saundarananda 9.21)
Whether you consider your strength to be great or not, engage first in battle with the sense-faculties;
for if you are victorious here, your strength is truly great, but if you are defeated, your strength is in vain.
Thus it is thought by the wise: those heroes who conquer the six senses, which are like iron, are truly victorious.
And as for your thought, "I am handsome," O discerning one—this is not so; let this also be grasped:
where is that beauty, and where are those beautiful bodies of Gada, Sāmba, and Sāraṇa? (Saundarananda 9.24)
Just as a peacock, with its shimmering variegated eye-patterns, possesses a form that is beautiful by its very nature, so too,
if you are truly possessed of beauty, you would possess such a form even without the quality of bodily adornment.

O handsome one, tell me, what would his body be like if he were to choose the contrary, if he did not touch water with his garment at the time of purification, or if he did not apply special ointments? *Saundarananda 9.26*

Observing that your youth has reached its prime, restrain that mind of yours which is turned toward home for the sake of attaining sensual pleasures; it is like the current of a mountain river, for youth passes away swiftly and without cessation.
The season that has passed returns again; the moon, having waned, comes back once more.
But the water of rivers and the youth of men, once gone, never returns. (Saundarananda 9.28)
When you behold your face discolored, with its beard faded, wrinkled and distorted, teeth decayed, eyebrows sagging, and devoid of luster—
worn out and overcome by old age— then you will be free from pride.
Having partaken of the finest intoxicating drink, a man may remain drunk for a long time even at the end of the night;
yet no man, intoxicated by his own strength, beauty, and youth, remains drunk until he has encountered old age.
Just as sugarcane, when its juice has been completely squeezed out and cast upon the ground, withers for the sake of being burned,
so too the body, crushed by the machine of old age and drained of its essence, remains only for death.
Just as a saw, when driven by two men, splits a towering piece of wood into many parts, so too does old age, joined with day and night, strike down this exalted generation. (Saundarananda 9.32)

The thief of memory, the destroyer of the body, the ender of pleasure, the captor of speech, hearing, and sight, the source of exhaustion, and the slayer of strength and vigor—for embodied beings, there is no enemy equal to old age. (Saundarananda 9.33)

Having understood this—the teacher of death, the great terror of the world that consumes with old age—you ought not to ascend to ignoble pride, thinking, "I am handsome, strong, and young. (Saundarananda 9.34)

For those whose minds are stained by the notions of "I" and "mine," there arises this perception of a body; O Kāla, abandon this grasping if you wish for peace to prevail, for it is through the notions of "I" and "mine" that fear is pursued.

When no one has mastery over the body as it is being assailed by various calamities, how can it be appropriate to regard this abode of misfortunes, known as the "body," as "I" or "mine"? (Saundarananda 9.36)

He who would always delight in a wretched house that is perpetually impure, yet constantly renovated and unsteady—he, possessing perverted vision, would delight in this body which is composed of foul elements, impure, and unstable. (Saundarananda 9.37)
Just as grasses sprout effortlessly upon the earth, whereas rice requires effort to grow; even so, sufferings like grass arise effortlessly, while those like rice may or may not arise through effort.

As one drags about this suffering body, which is unstable, there is nothing whatsoever that is ultimately happy. For what is called "happiness" is merely the pursuit of a remedy for suffering; and while suffering persists, it only subsides when that suffering has become diminished.
Just as even the slightest suffering that has arrived overcomes desired happiness regardless of its excellence,
so too, when suffering has come upon oneself, no happiness whatsoever exists for anyone, regardless of anything else.
If you do not realize that such a body is unstable and full of manifold sufferings for the sake of its fruits,
then let the mind be restrained from those fruits with the reins of fortitude, like a cow greedy for grain.
For sensual enjoyments do not lead to satisfaction, just as oblations do not satisfy a blazing fire;
in whatever measure one indulges in the pleasures of desire, to that same extent does longing for sense objects increase.
Just as one afflicted by the calamity of leprosy finds no relief from the burning heat,
so too one who wanders among the objects of the senses with uncontrolled faculties finds no peace through the enjoyment of desires.

For just as one might resort to diseases out of a desire for the pleasure of medicine, yet not resort to them when they have been cured, so too, though the body is a vessel of many sufferings, one might delight in it through delusion out of a longing for sense objects. (Saundarananda 9.45)
A person who desires what is harmful to another is indeed that person's enemy by virtue of that very act;
for sense objects are the sole root of harm and should surely be abandoned like dangerous enemies. (Saundarananda 9.46)
Having been enemies intent on destruction right here, they become friends to a person in the course of time;
yet sensual desires are the cause of suffering both in this world and the next, and are never auspicious for anyone. (Saundarananda 9.47)
Just as the fruit of the *kiṃpāka* tree, though possessing flavor, color, and fragrance, leads to death when consumed and not to nourishment;
so too do sense objects lead to misfortune and not to welfare for one whose mind is fickle.

Having understood this, which is free from evil, endowed with the dharma of liberation and other benefits, and is agreeable to the virtuous—either accept my opinion, or declare your own resolve by uttering your words. (Saundarananda 9.49)

Thus addressed by that great ascetic with words that were beneficial and abundant, Nanda neither attained steadfastness nor found peace; like an elephant blinded by rut and excessive passion, his mind was darkened by intoxication. (Saundarananda 9.50)

Having understood Nanda’s state of mind— which was wavering, directed toward domestic pleasures rather than the Dharma— the monk spoke to the Buddha, the knower of reality, who examines the dispositions, latent tendencies, and natures of sentient beings.

In the epic poem *Saundarananda*, the ninth canto, titled "The Refutation of Intoxication": Then, desiring to rescue Nanda—who was joyless, devoid of fortitude, having heard [the teaching] and wishing to cast off his virtuous vows, longing for his wife, and seeking to enter his home—the Sage summoned him. *Saundarananda* 10.1.
When he had arrived, his mind being pure, he asked him who had not yet attained the path of liberation about his lapse of thought;
bowing with modesty before that modest one, he spoke his own conviction to him who was skilled in discerning convictions.
Having perceived that Nanda was wandering in the darkness called "wife," the Sugata took him by the hand and leaped into the sky, like a virtuous man wishing to retrieve a jewel from the water.
Clad in saffron robes and radiant as gold, the two shone in the clear sky like a pair of ruddy geese with outspread wings joined together, gliding over a lake.

They quickly reached the Himavat, which possesses the supreme fragrance of *devadāru* trees, abounds in rivers, lakes, and cascading springs, contains veins of gold, and is frequented by divine sages.
On that auspicious mountain, frequented by Cāraṇas and Siddhas, where the smoke of sacrificial oblations served as a mantle,
those two arrived and stood like two islands in the sky, which is otherwise shoreless and without support.
While the Sage remained there with his senses stilled, Nanda gazed about in wonder at the caves,
the groves, and the forest-dwellers, who served as both the ornament and the protection of the mountain.
On that broad, white peak, a peacock lay with its plumage folded;
it shone like a beryl armlet upon the long, thick arm of Bala.
Resting upon a rock of red arsenic ore, the lion shone with his shoulders turned yellow,
like the shattered silver armlet of Ambika, once variegated with the patterns of refined gold.
Moving with a slow and playful gait like a tiger, his tail forming a circle as he swung it about,
he shone as he descended to the spring of Mount Prasravaṇa, desiring to drink water as if wishing to offer it to his ancestors.

On a tree with swaying kadamba flowers on its snowy slopes, a yak became entangled; though he wished to cut it loose, he was unable to sever the tail, just as a man of noble conduct cannot sever the affection born of his own kin.
And hosts of Kirātas, golden-hued, their bodies streaked with bright peacock feathers,
leaped from the caves like tigers pouncing, appearing like the outpouring of a mountain.
In every direction, throngs of kinnarīs—exceedingly beautiful, with enchanting hips, breasts, and necks—shone like flowering creepers with blossoms in their hair. (Saundarananda 10.13)
Monkeys roamed about, exhausting themselves by dragging *devadāru* trees from one mountain peak to another;
yet they obtained no fruit from them, just as those who place their hopes in lords whose favor is in vain.
Then, seeing that female monkey being driven away from the herd, her face stained with crushed red lac and one eye destroyed, the Sage spoke this to Nanda: *Saundarananda 10.15*
O Nanda, which do you consider more beautiful—this doe with her eyes darting and trembling, or that person toward whom your desire is directed? (Saundarananda 10.16)
Thus addressed by the Sugata, Nanda smiled slightly and spoke this:
"O Blessed One, where is that supreme woman, your bride, and where is this doe who causes distress to the mountain? (Saundarananda 10.17)
Then the Sage, having heard his words and perceiving some underlying motive,
took Nanda by the hand and proceeded just as before to the pleasure grove of King Vajradhara.

In that place, where the trees assume their form in each and every season at every single moment, some bear the manifold beauty of all six seasons together, while others display it individually. (Saundarananda 10.19)
Some prepared fragrant and magnificent garlands and various woven wreaths, as well as ear-ornaments suited to the ears, which seemed like rivals to their earrings. (Saundarananda 10.20)
Where the trees, with their red blossoming lotuses, shine like lamps upon poles;
and other trees, bearing blooming blue lotuses, appear as if their eyes were wide open.
There, the trees bear garments of various colors and white, illuminated by golden patterns; they are not woven from thread, being solid and fine.
[The trees also yield] necklaces, jewels, excellent earrings, the finest armlets, and anklets.
In that place, trees bear such ornaments as are worthy of heaven.
And lotus ponds with stalks of beryl, golden lotuses with diamond sprouts for filaments,
pleasant to the touch and possessing supreme fragrance, grow upon their unwavering surfaces.

There, trees variegated with jewels and gold—which serve as playmates for the inhabitants of the celestial abodes—bear as their fruit all those various musical instruments, both long and broad, whether hollow or solid. (Saundarananda 10.25)

Where that Pārijāta tree stands, shining with the qualities of its own majesty, it surpasses the mandāra trees, the kuśeśaya lotuses, and the kokanada trees bent down with blossoms, appearing like a king.
In that place, such trees that provide the enjoyments of the gods grow in succession, having been sown in the soil of the celestial field by the tireless ploughs of austerity and virtue.
Where the birds have faces like realgar, eyes resembling crystal,
and wings that are pale with crimson-tipped edges, and feet that are madder-red and half-white.
Others, birds known as śiñjikās, roam about with variegated golden wings and clear eyes the color of lapis lazuli, their songs captivating both the mind and the ear.
Where birds roam, adorned with creepers that are red at their tips, golden-yellow in their middles,
and the color of lapis lazuli in their inner sections.

Other winged creatures named Rociṣṇavas, with the color of blazing fire as if their mouths were aflame, wander about, captivating the eyes with their forms and stealing away the Apsarases with their auspicious songs. (Saundarananda 10.31)

There, those who perform meritorious deeds—whether inferior, superior, or middling—rejoice by virtue of their own actions; they move as they please, are perpetually joyful, free from affliction, free from decay, and free from sorrow, shining with their own radiance.
There, the playful apsarases captivate the weary minds of those rich in asceticism, who had previously resolved to purchase heaven by means of the price of their penance.

Beholding that world in perpetual festival, free from weariness, sleep, passion, grief, and disease, Nanda considered the world of men—subject to old age and death and ever-afflicted—to be like a cemetery. (Saundarananda 10.34)
And Nanda beheld that grove belonging to Indra, his eyes blossoming with wonder on every side;
and the Apsarases, filled with joy, surrounded him while looking at one another with pride.

Always youthful, with love as their sole pursuit, and common to all who have performed meritorious deeds, these divine women— free from the faults of worldly attachment— are the resort of the gods and the very foundation of the fruit of their asceticism.
Some sang in a steady, lofty tone; others gracefully plucked at lotuses;
and still others danced with mutual joy, their long rhythmic gestures causing the weight of their breasts to sway.
The faces of some among them, with their swaying earrings,
gleamed from within the forest like lotuses shaken by *kāraṇḍava* ducks emerging from mines where the leaves have been scattered.
Seeing them emerge from the depths of the forest like streaks of lightning from rain-clouds,
Nanda’s body trembled with passion, like the reflection of the moon in rippling water.
Then, by means of their divine form and graceful movements, he captivated their minds;
and with eyes drawn by curiosity, he felt passion as if from a thirst for union.
His thirst having been aroused, longing to drink in the Apsarases and striving to attain them with a heart distressed by agitation,
he could find no steadfastness as he was dragged along by the chariot of his mind, which has the restless senses for its horses.

Just as a person makes a soiled garment even dirtier with alkaline salt—not for the sake of removing the stain, but rather for the purpose of producing more grime—so did the Sage draw forth passion from him. (Saundarananda 10.42)
Just as a physician, desiring to extract humors from the body, might strive to afflict it further,
so the Sage, wishing to destroy his passion, induced even greater passion within him.
Just as the radiance of the thousand-rayed sun rising in the darkness eclipses the light of a lamp,
so does the splendor of the apsarases obscure the beauty of women in the world of men.
A great form destroys a small form, and a loud sound destroys a faint sound;
a severe pain destroys a mild pain—every great cause leads to the destruction of the small. (Saundarananda 10.45)
And by the power of the Sage, Nanda was able to endure that sight, which others could not bear;
for the beauty of the bodies of the apsarases would burn the mind of one who is weak and not free from passion. (Saundarananda 10.46)

Then, perceiving that Nanda’s passion was aroused while his own passion for his wife had ceased, the dispassionate Sage, desiring to counteract passion with passion, spoke these words: Saundarananda 10.47.
"Look at these women, O inhabitant of heaven; having observed them, speak the truth:
how are they regarded by you in terms of beauty and virtue, or what is that person to whom your mind has gone? (Saundarananda 10.48)

Then Nanda, his gaze fixed upon the apsarases, his inner heart set ablaze by the fire of passion, and his mind clinging to desire, spoke these words with a faltering voice while joining his palms in reverence: *Saundarananda 10.49*
O Lord, while that woman with beautiful limbs and stolen gaze might be within your reach,
in that very interval, that wretched wife of yours will have fallen for the celestial nymphs of your court.
Just as I previously had no regard for any other women once I had beheld my wife, so now I have no regard at all for her once I have beheld the beauty of these others. (Saundarananda 10.51)
Just as someone who has been scorched by a mild heat might be burned by a great fire, so too,
having first been tormented by mild passion, I am now being consumed by this fire of passion.
Therefore, sprinkle me with the water of your words before I am consumed by that fire which is like the enemy of the lotus;
for today this blazing fire desires to burn me, just as a rising fire consumes dry wood along with the tops of the trees. (Saundarananda 10.53)

Be gracious; I am sinking, O Sage, release me! O you whose fortitude is like the earth, I possess no fortitude. I shall give up my life, O one whose mind is liberated; or else, grant the nectar of your words to one who is about to die.

For I have been bitten in the heart by the serpent of passion, which brings about the enjoyment of what is useless, whose gaze is calamity, whose fangs are negligence, and whose venomous fire is darkness; therefore, O Great Physician, please provide the antidote for it. (Saundarananda 10.55)
For no man bitten by this serpent of passion remains steady in himself;
indeed, the mind of Bodhya, though firm of soul, was deluded, and the wise Śantanu became emaciated in body.
Since you, the distinguished refuge, are present, I take my shelter so that, while dwelling here, I do not wander from direction to direction;
and so that, having attained the end of my calamities, I may reach my final rest—grant this for me as I speak thus, being one who is virtuous.

Then Gautama, the moon among great seers who dispels the darkness of the world and has abandoned all darkness, spoke to him as he sought to strike his heart— just as the sun, the dispeller of darkness, rises at night against the rising gloom.
Embracing fortitude, shaking off agitation, and restraining both your learning and your mind, listen:
if you desire these women, then perform supreme austerity here as the price for them. (Saundarananda 10.59)

For these cannot be won by force, nor by service, nor by giving, nor by physical beauty; indeed, they are carried away solely by the practice of Dharma. Therefore, if you have joy, practice the Dharma with reverence.

Dwelling here in heaven together with the gods, amidst delightful forests and ageless women—this is the fruit of one's own auspicious karma; it was not given by another, nor did it arise without a cause. (Saundarananda 10.61)
On earth, a man may perhaps obtain women through the toil of bows and other such efforts, or he may not;
but those who perform meritorious deeds here undoubtedly become [the consorts] of one of virtuous conduct in heaven. (Saundarananda 10.62)
Therefore, being vigilant and diligent in your observance, take delight if you desire the celestial nymphs;
and I shall stand as your guarantor that, provided your vow remains firm, you will certainly be reunited with them.
From that point on, established in the thought that this was the supreme [state], he exercised the highest resolve toward the Supreme Sage.
Then the Sage, descending like the wind from the sky, took hold of him and returned once more to the surface of the earth. (Saundarananda 10.64)
In the epic poem *Saundarananda*, the tenth canto, titled "The Vision of Heaven," [ends here].
Then, having seen those women wandering in the Nandana grove, Nanda bound his restless and difficult-to-tame mind to the pillar of self-restraint. (*Saundarananda* 11.1)
Having fixed the celestial nymphs in his heart, he wandered about practicing the Dharma devoid of flavor, like a withered lotus, his taste for the essence of renunciation lost.
Likewise, having been one whose senses were restless and whose range of sensory experience was dear to him,
he became one whose senses were restrained solely through mastery over the objects of the senses.
Skilled in the ways of sensual pleasure yet faltering in the conduct of a monk,
he practiced the holy life, supported by his supreme teacher.
Through the restraint of his peaceful mind and the intensity of his passion,
he was both cooled and consumed, like the meeting of water and fire.
Although he was naturally handsome, he became exceedingly unsightly due to his brooding over the apsarases and because of his long-standing ascetic discipline.
Even during conversations concerning his wife, though he was a lover of his wife, he rose up as if free from passion; he neither rejoiced nor was he agitated.
Perceiving that he was thus established and turned away from passion for his wife, Ānanda approached Nanda and spoke these words out of affection: *Saundarananda 11.8*
Oh, how worthy of his learning and noble lineage is this undertaking!
For he has restrained his senses, remains composed, and is firmly established in his discipline.
That this consciousness has arisen in one who is intensely attached to desires, impassioned, and whose soul is fixed on sense-objects, could not have been caused by a minor reason.
A mild disease is warded off with little effort;
a powerful one perishes—or perhaps does not—only through powerful efforts. (Saundarananda 11.11)
The mental affliction that you possessed was powerful and difficult to remove;
if it has been turned back from you, then in every respect you are steadfast.
It is difficult for one who is ignoble to achieve excellence, and for one who is proud to achieve gentleness;
it is difficult for one who is greedy to practice renunciation, and for one who is passionate to observe celibacy.
But I have one doubt regarding this firm resolve of yours; I desire your consent in this matter, if it is something you would deign to say. (Saundarananda 11.14)
A word spoken with sincerity must not be taken otherwise; for a virtuous person does not perceive even harshness as harshness when the underlying intention is pure. (Saundarananda 11.15)
For that which is pleasant is beneficial, while that which is unpleasant may be beneficial;
and that which is both pleasant and beneficial is difficult to find, like medicine that is both delicious and wholesome. (Saundarananda 11.16)
Trust, acting for one's welfare, sharing in both joy and sorrow,
forbearance, and affection— this is the conduct of friendship among the virtuous.
Therefore, I wish to speak this to you out of affection, not with a desire to harm;
for my intention is to speak what is for your own welfare, since I ought not to remain indifferent.
"You are said to practice the Dharma while being a hireling of the Apsarases; is this a reality, or is it such a joke? (Saundarananda 11.19)
If what I am about to say here is true, I shall speak it; if, on the other hand, it is mere boastfulness, I shall speak it according to the truth. (Saundarananda 11.20)
Then, though struck in the heart by him with gentle words, he reflected for a long time, sighed deeply, and turned his face slightly downward. (Saundarananda 11.21)
Then, having perceived his gesture which indicated the resolve of his mind, Ānanda spoke words that were unpleasant yet sweet in their ultimate consequence. (Saundarananda 11.22)
From your appearance, I perceive your purpose regarding the Dharma;
knowing which, both laughter and compassion have arisen within me toward you. (Saundarananda 11.23)
Just as someone might carry a heavy stone on their shoulder for the sake of a seat,
so too are you prepared to bear this restraint for the sake of sensual desires.
Just as a ram retreats when another approaches with the desire to strike it,
so too is this celibacy of yours for the sake of non-celibacy.
Just as merchants desire to sell their merchandise out of a longing for profit, so too is your practice of dharma like a commodity; it does not lead to peace.
Just as a farmer sows seed for the sake of a specific fruit,
so too have you abandoned sense objects out of a longing for those very objects.
Just as one might desire a disease out of a longing for the pleasure of its remedy,
so do you seek suffering through craving for sense objects.
Just as one sees only the honey and does not look toward the precipice,
so do you see the celestial nymphs and fail to see your fall at the end.
With the fire of desire blazing in your heart, though you bear the vow with your body,
what is this celibacy of yours, O non-celibate one, if it exists only in mind?
Since you have lived in saṃsāra, hundreds of apsarases have been obtained by you and abandoned; why, then, do you still feel desire for them? (Saundarananda 11.31)

Fire is not satisfied by fuel, nor the salt-water ocean by water; likewise, one who possesses thirst is not satisfied by sensual pleasures. Therefore, desires do not lead to contentment. (Saundarananda 11.32)

And where is there peace for one who is insatiable? And where is there happiness for one who lacks peace? Where is there joy for one who lacks happiness? And where is there delight for one who lacks joy? (Saundarananda 11.33)
If you desire to sport, therefore let your mind be fixed upon the inner self;
for there is no delight equal to that of the inner self, which is tranquil and blameless.
There, you have no need for musical instruments, nor for women, nor for ornaments;
for wherever you abide, you shall find delight through that alone.
Mental suffering remains powerful as long as craving persists;
therefore, cut off that craving, for suffering exists only where there is craving, whether it be present or absent.
Whether in prosperity or in adversity, by day or by night,
for one who craves sensual pleasures, peace is never attained.
The longing for sensual pleasures is suffering; there is no satisfaction even when they are attained.
Separation from them inevitably brings grief, and separation is certain even in heaven. (Saundarananda 11.38)
Even after performing difficult deeds and attaining the rare heaven,
he returns once more to the world of men, just as one returns from abroad to his own home.
When no wholesome merit remains for one who has fallen away,
he is reborn among the three types of ghosts, in the world of the ancestors, or in hell.
For him who has enjoyed even the most excellent objects of sense in heaven,
but has now fallen and is afflicted by suffering— what pleasure can that [former enjoyment] provide?
Out of compassion for living beings, Śibi gave even his own flesh to the hawk;
yet, despite performing such a difficult deed, he fell from heaven. (Saundarananda 11.42)
Having occupied half of Śakra’s throne, he who was indeed a former king returned once more to the lower world when the time for the gods had passed— Māndhātṛ.
Even after ruling over the gods, Nahuṣa fell to the earth;
it is said that he attained the state of a serpent and is not yet released from it even today.
In the same way, King Elivila, though refined by the conduct of a king,
went to heaven but fell from there again, it is said, having become a tortoise in the ocean.
Bhūriyaśas, Yayāti, and those other bulls among kings,
having purchased heaven by means of their deeds, abandoned it once again upon its exhaustion.
But the Asuras, their splendor having been taken away by the gods,
fled to Pātāla for refuge, grieving for that lost glory.
Moreover, even by royal sages, or by asuras, or by gods and others, hundreds of great Indras have fallen; thus, even majesty is not stable. (Saundarananda 11.48)
Having graced the assembly of Indra, Upendra Trivikrama,
his karma exhausted, descended into the midst of the Apsarases, making them resound with joy.
"Alas, Caitraratha! Alas, the pond! Alas, Mandākinī!
Alas, my beloved!"—thus the denizens of heaven fall to the earth, lamenting in their distress.
For even here, intense suffering arises for those about to die;
how much more so for those who, having indulged in pleasure, fall at last from heaven itself? (Saundarananda 11.51)
Dust clings to the garments, the finest garlands wither, sweat breaks out from the limbs, and there is no pleasure in sitting. (Saundarananda 11.52)
These were the first signs of the fall from heaven for the celestial dwellers,
like the undesirable omens of death for mortals who are about to die.
Whatever happiness arises for those enjoying sensual pleasures in heaven,
and whatever suffering there is for those falling [from it], that suffering alone remains distinct.
Therefore, having realized that heaven is devoid of essence, provides no protection, is untrustworthy, fails to satisfy, and is subject to decay, set your mind upon liberation.
For although the sage Udraka reached the formless realm of the Peak of Existence,
at the end of his karma he fell from there and will enter the womb of an animal.
Through seven years of loving-kindness, Sunetra departed from here for the Brahma-world;
yet he returned once more and entered the dwelling of a womb.

And when even those dwelling in heaven, though possessing sovereignty, are subject to decay, what wise person indeed would long for a heavenly residence that is destined to perish? (Saundarananda 11.58)
Just as a bird bound by a string returns again and again even though it has flown far away,
so too does the world, bound by the string of ignorance, return once more even though it has gone far.
Just as one who has deceived the timekeeper is released from bondage by a surety, yet after enjoying the pleasures of his house and the lapse of the agreed period, enters bondage once again;

even so, having reached heaven through self-restraints such as meditation—which act like a surety—when the time comes and those objects of experience resulting from karma have been enjoyed, he is dragged back again to the earth.
Just as fish within a net in a pond, their minds heedless, do not perceive the calamity born of their confinement and move about freely in the water;

so too those who have entered the inner worlds, believing their purpose is accomplished, imagine their own abode—which is subject to return—to be auspicious, imperishable, and eternal, even as they meditate upon heaven.

Perceiving this world to be encompassed by birth, disease, death, and calamity, wandering through cyclic existence among gods, humans, hell-beings, animals, and ancestors, practice the holy life for the sake of that which is a fearless refuge, auspicious, immortal, ageless, sorrowless, and deathless; abandon your longing for the fickle heaven.
In the epic poem *Saundarananda*, the eleventh canto, titled "The Denunciation of Heaven":
Then, having been addressed by Ānanda, "Nanda, you practice the Dharma as a hireling for the Apsarases," Nanda was overcome with the utmost shame. (Saundarananda 12.1)
Due to his great shame, no joy arose in his heart; because of his lack of delight, his mind turned away from and did not remain fixed upon his vow.
Although he was dominated by sensual passion and even treated it as a mere jest,
he could not endure those words once the cause had reached its full maturity.
And because he had previously considered heaven to be eternal due to a lack of investigation,
he now experienced intense agitation upon hearing that it was subject to decay.
His desire for heaven, which had been like a horse of resolve, turned back from its course—
just as a great chariot is turned from a wrong path by an attentive charioteer.
Having turned away from his thirst for heaven, he immediately became as if restored to health;
like a sick man desiring to live who has abstained from delicious but unwholesome food.
Just as he had forgotten his beloved wife upon seeing the Apsarases,
so too, agitated by the thought of impermanence, did he abandon even the Apsarases.
Reflecting that even for great beings there is rebirth,
he became like one free from passion through his sense of urgency, even though he was still possessed of passion.
For that spiritual urgency arose for the increase of his welfare, just as the root *edh* is recited by those who study the alphabet among the verbal roots. (Saundarananda 12.9)

But his mind was not captivated by sensual desires; his steadfastness remained unshaken at all times, in all circumstances, like the verb *as* ("to be") which is understood even when not explicitly stated.
Moving with a playful gait, the mighty-armed one, like a rutting lord of elephants,
approached his teacher at the proper time, desiring to express his inner state.
Having bowed his head to the Guru, his eyes clouded with tears, he joined his palms in reverence and, with his face slightly cast down in shame, spoke these words. (Saundarananda 12.12)
"O Blessed One, since you were my guarantor for the attainment of apsarases, I have no need for the apsarases; I renounce your status as my guarantor. (Saundarananda 12.13)
For having heard of the revolving nature of heaven and the diversity of saṃsāra, neither among mortals nor among gods does active engagement appeal to me. (Saundarananda 12.14)
If, having attained heaven through effort, self-restraint, and discipline, they fall at the end still unsatisfied, then homage to the one who gives for the sake of heaven! *Saundarananda* 12.15.
And therefore, having understood the entire world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
I take delight in your supreme Dharma, which brings about the destruction of all suffering.
Therefore, O best of listeners, you should explain it to me both in detail and in brief, so that by hearing it, I may attain the supreme state. (Saundarananda 12.17)
Then, having understood his disposition, his faculties, and the obstacles [to his progress],
as well as the spiritual welfare that had become manifest before him, the Tathāgata spoke.
"Aha! This reflective discernment of yours is a precursor to the highest good, rising like smoke from fire when the fire-drill is being rubbed in the forest. (Saundarananda 12.19)
Having wandered for a long time on the wrong path with the restless horses of the senses,
you have fortunately descended onto the right path by means of your unclouded vision.
Today your birth has borne fruit; today you have attained a most great gain, you whose mind, though knowing the flavor of desire, yearns for renunciation.
In this world, which delights in the storehouse-consciousness (ālaya), joy in cessation is difficult to find;
for fools tremble at the state of non-rebirth as if at a precipice.
People strive with the thought, "May there be no suffering; may there be happiness for me";
yet they do not understand that true happiness is the absolute cessation of suffering. (Saundarananda 12.23)
The world is attached to impermanent beings and to desires and the like, which are constant causes of suffering; it does not know the imperishable bliss. (Saundarananda 12.24)
That nectar, which removes all suffering, is now in your hand;
for you wish to drink the antidote at the proper time after having drunk poison.
O you who are worthy of honor, your intended deed is worthy of praise, for it dispels the fear of an unworthy saṃsāra;
such is the fire of passion that it turns away from one whose face is set toward the Dharma.
With a mind frenzied by passion, steadfastness is altogether difficult to maintain,
just as it is for a thirsty traveler who sees water tainted with poison.
Such was your intellect, now obstructed by passion (rajas), like the radiance of the sun obscured by a fierce wind. (Saundarananda 12.28)
Desiring to destroy the darkness within the heart, she who now unfolds herself is like the solar radiance vomited forth by Mount Meru to dispel the darkness of night.
And this is indeed appropriate for a mind of pure being: that you should have faith in the ultimate, subtle, and supreme good. (Saundarananda 12.30)
Therefore, you ought to increase this desire for the Dharma;
for, O Knower of Dharma, all phenomena are by necessity the causes of desire.
For when the cognition of going is present, one proceeds to go;
likewise, when there is the cognition of lying down, one lies down, and when there is the cognition of standing, one stands.
When a person has faith that water exists within the earth, then, being in need of it, they dig into this ground with effort. (Saundarananda 12.33)
If one were not desirous of fire, one would not have faith in the two kindling-sticks;
nor would anyone rub the kindling-stick if that [desire] were absent; yet, when that state exists, it is rubbed. (Saundarananda 12.34)
If a farmer did not have faith in the growth of crops in the earth, or if he were not desirous of the crop, he would not sow seeds in the ground. (Saundarananda 12.35)
And for this reason, I have specifically called faith "the hand," because it grasps the true Dharma as an unimpaired hand takes a gift.

Because of its preeminence it is called a faculty (*indriya*); because of its stability it is called strength (*bala*); and because it pacifies the poverty of qualities, it is described as wealth (*dhana*). (Saundarananda 12.37)
Because it serves to protect the Dharma, it is called "the reed-shaft" (iṣīkā); and because it is difficult to find in this world, it is designated as a "jewel" (ratna). (Saundarananda 12.38)
Furthermore, she is called "seed" because she is the cause for the arising of excellence;
and again, she is designated as a "river" in the sense that she purifies evil.
Since faith is the supreme cause for the arising of the Dharma,
I have therefore described it in various ways according to its effects in those respective instances.
Therefore, you ought to nurture this sprout of faith;
for when it grows, Dharma increases, just as a tree does when its roots grow.
He whose vision is confused and whose resolve is weak possesses a wavering faith; indeed, such faith does not persist once it has been formed.
As long as reality has not been seen or heard, faith does not become strong or firm;
but when reality is seen, for one whose senses have been subdued by self-restraint, the tree of faith bears fruit and provides a secure refuge.
The twelfth canto, titled "Reflection," in the epic poem *Saundarananda*.
Then Nanda, having been won over by the great seer regarding faith, was as if sprinkled with nectar and joined with supreme joy. *Saundarananda* 13.1.
Through that faith, the Fully Awakened One considered him as one who had already accomplished his purpose;
and he, refined by the Buddha, considered that the highest good had been attained.
That leader disciplined some with gentle words, some with harsh speech, and others with both of these methods. (Saundarananda 13.3)
Just as gold, born from dust, is pure, stainless, and clean, and even while remaining amidst the dust, it is not defiled by the defects of the dust; so too is the Tathāgata. 13.4
Just as a lotus leaf, though born in the water and situated in the water,
is not defiled by the water from above or below, so too is he.
In the same way, the sage born in the world, practicing for the benefit of the world,
is not defiled by worldly conditions because of his perfected state and his stainless purity.
At the time of reproaching him for the sake of medical treatment, he employed endearment, abandonment, pleasantness, harshness, discourse, and even meditation; he did not act out of self-indulgence.
And therefore, out of that great compassion, he, being full of pity, resolved upon his inheritance: "How might I liberate sentient beings from suffering? (Saundarananda 13.8)
Then, perceiving that Nanda had been gladdened and made a fit vessel,
he who was the best among speakers and knew the sequence of the highest goods spoke regarding the sequence of those things leading to welfare.
From this point forward, O gentle one, you should once again, with faith as your foremost guide,
strive to maintain your conduct for the attainment of the deathless state.
"Practice such that your conduct of body and speech becomes pure; act so that it is open, restrained, guarded, and without flaw. (Saundarananda 13.11)
It is "upturned" because it produces a state of being; "uncovered" because it is not concealed;
"guarded" because of its intent toward protection; and "without flaw" because it is irreproachable.
For the purification of body and speech, and also for the sevenfold action,
you ought to refine your livelihood and conduct through purity.
By not indulging in the five faults such as hypocrisy and the like, and by abandoning the four destroyers of livelihood, such as astrology and so forth. (Saundarananda 13.14)
Because he did not accept prohibited things such as living beings, vows, or wealth, and because he accepted the prescribed and fixed requisites for a mendicant; Saund_13.15 //
Rising early, pure, and gentle, with a clean endowment of livelihood,
one should apply remedies for suffering only so far as it leads to liberation.
For although livelihood arises from the same source as bodily and vocal actions—as seen in the case of karma—I have taught it separately because it is so difficult to purify. (Saundarananda 13.17)

For the view of a householder is difficult to purify when one holds various views, and the livelihood of a monk is likewise difficult when his conduct depends on the favor of others. (Saundarananda 13.18)
This much has been called morality; this is conduct in brief.
Through its destruction, there would be neither the state of a renunciant nor that of a householder. (Saundarananda 13.19)
Therefore, endowed with right conduct, practice this holy life,
perceiving danger even in the slightest faults and remaining firm in your vows.
For all activities leading to the highest good proceed by relying upon ethical discipline,
just as all tasks such as standing and moving depend upon the earth as their foundation.

"O gentle one, let it be understood that detachment is the secret essence of liberation; the secret essence of detachment is self-awareness, and the secret essence of self-awareness is the vision of knowledge. (Saundarananda 13.22)
Let it be understood that the secret essence of knowledge is meditative concentration;
and the secret essence of meditative concentration is physical and mental happiness.
Tranquility of body and mind is the supreme proximate cause of happiness;
and joy is considered by me to be the supreme proximate cause of tranquility.
Likewise, joy is considered the secret essence of gladness; and the absence of remorse regarding what was poorly done or left undone is the secret essence of joy. (Saundarananda 13.25)
The pure secret essence of the mind that is free from mental impressions is ethical discipline;
therefore, since discipline leads to the highest state, purify your ethical discipline.
It is called "śīla" (virtue) because of its cultivation; cultivation arises from practice, practice from following instructions, and instruction from taking that [virtue] as one's refuge.
For ethical conduct, O gentle one, is a refuge like a guide in a wilderness;
it is a friend, a kinsman, a protection, wealth, and indeed a strength. (Saundarananda 13.28)
Therefore, O gentle one, you ought to cultivate moral conduct;
for this is the foundation, as well as other [qualities], for yogins at the commencement of the pursuit of liberation.
Therefore, establishing yourself in mindfulness, you ought to restrain the senses, which are by their very nature fickle, from the objects of the senses.
One should not fear an enemy, nor fire, nor a serpent, nor lightning as much as one should fear one's own senses; for by them one is constantly struck down.
Sometimes someone is afflicted by enemies, or perhaps not; but everyone is oppressed by the senses everywhere and at all times. (Saundarananda 13.32)
One who is slain by enemies and the like does not go to hell;
however, one who is helpless, being struck down by the fickle senses, is dragged there.
For one being struck by those [afflictions], there may or may not be mental suffering;
but for one oppressed by the sense faculties, there is both mental and physical suffering.
For the arrows consisting of the five senses are smeared with the poison of volition;
they have thought for their shafts, passion for their fruit, and range through the space of the sense-objects.
Driven by the hunter that is desire, they strike human deer in the heart;
if they do not kill them, the deer fall, wounded by those very arrows.
Stationed upon the courtyard of self-restraint, wielding the bow of fortitude and clad in the great armor of mindfulness, they must be warded off as they fall.
Through the pacification of the senses, as if through the subduing of enemies,
he sleeps or sits at ease wherever he may go, his agitation having departed.
For those who constantly crave sense-objects in this world, there is no true awareness due to their wretchedness, just like that of dogs full of longing. (Saundarananda 13.39)
The host of sense-faculties finds no satisfaction through sensory objects, just as the ocean, though being filled incessantly, is never satiated by waters. (Saundarananda 13.40)
In this world, the sense faculties must necessarily operate within their respective domains;
however, one should not grasp at the primary signs therein, nor even at the secondary characteristics. Saundarananda 13.41.
Having perceived a form with the eye, established in the mere elements, you should not conceptualize it as "a woman" or "a man. (Saundarananda 13.42)
If some grasping for "woman" or "man" should exist anywhere at all,
you ought not to pursue the hair, teeth, and so forth as being beautiful.
That which is real should not be removed from its reality within the range of the senses;
rather, that which is real should be seen as it truly is, according to its nature, and in whatever manner it exists.
Thus, as you constantly perceive reality within the range of the senses,
there will be no foothold for dejection or mental distress.

Covetousness, appearing in a pleasing form, destroys the world whose nature is desire, just as an enemy with a friend’s face destroys one who is pure-hearted through pleasant speech. (Saundarananda 13.46)
But resentment, which is designated as mental distress, is based on sense objects;
through its persistence out of delusion, one is destroyed both in this world and in the next.
Afflicted by likes and dislikes as if by cold and heat, the world with its unsteady senses finds neither comfort nor the highest good; therefore, it does not attain liberation.
The sense faculty does not become attached to its object, even though it has engaged with it,
as long as conceptual construction of the mind does not operate therein.
Just as fire blazes when there is fuel and wind,
so too does the fire of the afflictions arise from sense objects and conceptual construction.
For one is bound by the object through unreal imagination;
seeing that very same object as it truly is, one is completely liberated.
For upon seeing a single form, one person becomes impassioned, another becomes repelled, someone else remains neutral, and yet another feels loathing for that very same thing. (Saundarananda 13.52)
Therefore, the object is neither a cause for bondage nor for liberation;
attachment arises or does not arise depending on the particularity of one's conceptual construction.
Therefore, restraint of the senses should be practiced with the utmost effort;
for the senses, when left unguarded, lead to suffering and to continued existence.

By the serpents of the senses—those who enjoy the pleasures of desire, whose eyes are fixed on objects of sense, whose single heads are heedlessness, whose flickering tongues are intense longing, and who dwell in the hollow of the mind—there is no bite that cannot be treated except by the medicine of tranquility. (Saundarananda 13.55)

Therefore, being vigilant at all times by restraining these enemies that produce unwholesome states—the eye, nose, ear, tongue, and body—do not, for even a moment, allow yourself to be negligent in this matter. (Saundarananda 13.56)
The thirteenth canto, titled "The Conquest of the Senses through Moral Conduct," from the *Saundarananda* Mahākāvya:
Now, having closed the door of mindfulness over the restraint of the senses, be moderate in eating for the sake of meditation and health. (Saundarananda 14.1)
It restrains the out-breath and in-breath, brings on exhaustion and sleep, and when food is taken in excess, it destroys one's vigor. (Saundarananda 14.2)
Just as food taken in excess leads to misfortune, so too food consumed in too small a measure does not lead to strength. (Saundarananda 14.3)
Food that has been eaten in too small a quantity diminishes one's accumulation, radiance, enthusiasm, application, and even physical strength. (Saundarananda 14.4)
Just as a scale bends down with a heavy load and rises with a light one,
so does this body remain balanced through appropriate food.
Therefore, observing one's own capacity, one should consume food that is neither excessive nor too small, even if it is measured according to the rules for human beings.
For the bodily fire, when overwhelmed by heavy food, is extinguished like a small fire suddenly covered with a great quantity of fuel. (Saundarananda 14.7)
Even a complete cessation of food is not recommended;
for by abstaining from food, one attains extinction like a fire without fuel.
Since there is no subsistence for any living beings without food, therefore food itself is not blameworthy; rather, it is the conceptual attachment to it that is to be restrained.
For living beings do not become so attached to other objects as they are to food when it is unknown; one should understand that this is the reason in that case.
Just as one who has a wound applies an ointment for the sake of healing, so too should food be consumed by one seeking liberation for the sake of warding off hunger. (Saundarananda 14.11)
Just as the axle of a chariot is lubricated for the purpose of bearing a heavy load, so too does the wise man partake of food for the sake of sustaining life. (Saundarananda 14.12)
And just as two travelers, for the sake of crossing a wilderness,
might eat the flesh of their own son, so did the husband and wife, though deeply distressed, consume it.
In this way, food should be consumed with discernment:
not for the sake of adornment, nor for the sake of physical beauty, nor for intoxication, nor for pride.
For food is prescribed for the sake of sustaining the body, like a prop for a weak house that is about to collapse. (Saundarananda 14.15)

Just as someone might laboriously tie together and hold onto a raft—not out of affection for it, but solely with the desire to cross over a great flood—so too [should one hold onto the teachings]. (Saundarananda 14.16)
In the same way, those who examine [the body] sustain it with its requisites not out of affection for it, but rather from the desire to cross over the flood of suffering. (Saundarananda 14.17)
Just as one who is grieving and oppressed gives to an enemy neither out of devotion nor out of longing, but solely for the sake of protecting his life; so it is here.
In this way, the practitioner of yoga provides food for the body solely for the purpose of warding off hunger, neither out of passion nor for the sake of physical beauty.
And by means of mental concentration, the self-possessed one,
having dispelled sleep through yoga, should pass even the night in transformation.
If sleep should arise in your heart while you are conscious,
then do not form the notion in your mind that it is a state characterized by the [mental] qualities.
You who are being oppressed by sleep must always cultivate in your mind the element of resolve, as well as steadfastness, endurance, and valor. (Saundarananda 14.22)
Those teachings which you have heard should be clearly committed to memory;
they should be taught to others and reflected upon by yourself as well. (Saundarananda 14.23)
One desiring to remain awake should always look at the face moistened with water, gaze in all directions, and direct the vision toward the stars. (Saundarananda 14.24)
With your senses withdrawn, steady, and remaining under control,
and with a mind undistracted, walk about or sit at night.
In fear, in joy, and in sorrow, one is not overcome by sleep;
therefore, when sleepiness assails, these three should be practiced.
You ought to experience fear from the arrival of death, joy from the embrace of Dharma, and sorrow from the boundless suffering of birth. (Saundarananda 14.27)
O gentle one, such a sequence should be followed regarding the vigil; for what wise person would allow life to become fruitless through sleep? (Saundarananda 14.28)
Having transcended the serpents of the defilements as if they were snakes within one's own home,
it is not fitting for a wise man who seeks to cross over this great terror to sleep.
For when the world of living beings is ablaze with the fires of death, disease, and old age, who could lie down without agitation, as if in a burning house? (Saundarananda 14.30)
Therefore, knowing it to be darkness, you ought not to embrace sleep while the faults remain unappeased, like enemies bearing weapons.
Having passed the first watch of the three-watch night through spiritual practice, one who is self-reliant should resort to a bed for the sake of resting the body. (Saundarananda 14.32)
But lying on your right side with the perception of light,
you should sleep with a tranquil mind, having brought awakening to your heart.
And having risen in the third watch of the night, whether walking or sitting,
you should once again practice yoga for the sake of great purification, with your senses restrained.
Furthermore, when sitting, standing, looking about, speaking, and so forth, you ought to maintain mindfulness with full awareness in all your actions. (Saundarananda 14.35)
Just as enemies cannot overcome a guarded city, so faults do not overcome him whose mindfulness is stationed at the gateway like a gatekeeper. (Saundarananda 14.36)
Affliction does not arise for one whose mindfulness is directed toward the body;
in all circumstances, it protects the mind like a nurse protects an infant.
But he who is devoid of the armor of mindfulness is a target for faults, like a warrior standing in battle without his armor against his enemies. (Saundarananda 14.38)
That mind should be known as unprotected which mindfulness does not guard;
it is like a leader devoid of vision wandering among treacherous terrains. (Saundarananda 14.39)
Attached to what is meaningless and turned away from their own true welfare, they are not agitated even when danger is present; in this case, the loss of mindfulness is the cause.
Mindfulness follows those virtues—such as ethical discipline and the rest—which reside within their own respective stages, just as a cowherd follows his scattered cattle. (Saundarananda 14.41)
The nectar of immortality is lost for him whose mindfulness has strayed far away;
the nectar of immortality is held in his hand by him whose mindfulness is established within the body.
Whence can there be noble method for one in whom mindfulness is not found?
And for one who has no noble method, the true path is lost. (Saundarananda 14.43)
For one whose true path is lost, the immortal state is lost;
for one whose immortal state is lost, he is not released from suffering. (Saundarananda 14.44)
Therefore, whether moving with the thought "I am moving" or standing still with the thought "I am standing," you ought to maintain mindfulness during such times as these. (Saundarananda 14.45)
O gentle one, resort to a secluded lodging that is free from noise and conducive to sacrifice;
for having first achieved physical seclusion, it is easy to attain mental seclusion.
He who has not attained tranquility of mind and is still possessed by passion does not resort to a secluded course of conduct;
for he is worn out like one traveling on a road full of thorns without having found a path.
For an investigator who has not seen reality, while remaining amidst the manifold movement of sense objects,
it is not easy to restrain the mind, like a bull that has been dragged away from the midst of the crops.
Just as a fire, when not fanned by the wind, comes to a state of calm, so too the mind, when undisturbed in solitary places, attains peace with little effort. (Saundarananda 14.49)
Having eaten whatever food at any place, and having worn whatever garment at any time,
he who dwells delighting in the Self in some solitary spot is to be known as one who has accomplished his purpose— one who knows the flavor of the bliss of tranquility and possesses a perfected mind.
He avoids association with others as if they were a thorn. (Saundarananda 14.50)
If, while the world delights in dualities and its hearts are distracted by sense objects, the accomplished one with a peaceful heart dwells in solitude free from duality;
then, having drunk the essence of wisdom like nectar, his heart is satisfied.
Detached himself, he grieved for the world that was attached and miserable in its pursuit of sense objects.
If one constantly dwells in an empty house and finds delight therein alone;
if one does not take pleasure in the arising of afflictions as if they were enemies;
and if, wandering while rejoicing in the self, one drinks the water of joy—then [one is a true ascetic].
Thereupon he enjoys a supreme happiness, even greater than the sovereignty of the Lord of the Thirty-three.
The fourteenth canto, titled "The Initial Departure," from the epic poem *Saundarananda*:
In various secluded places, having assumed the supreme cross-legged posture, he set his body straight and was endowed with mindfulness directed forward. (Saundarananda 15.1)
One should make the restless mind intent upon an object of focus at the tip of the nose, or on the forehead, or indeed between the eyebrows. (Saundarananda 15.2)
If a thought of sensual desire should overcome you— a fever of the mind—
it must be cast away and not tolerated, like dust that has settled upon a garment.
Even though you have abandoned sensual desires through discernment,
destroy them with their antidote, as one destroys darkness with light.
The latent tendency of those [passions] remains, like fire covered by ashes;
O gentle one, it must be extinguished by you through meditative cultivation, as fire is quenched by water. (Saundarananda 15.5)
For they proceed from that [mind] again, like sprouts from a seed;
by its destruction, they would not exist, just as sprouts do not exist when the seed is destroyed.
Having seen that for those possessed by desire, acquisition and the like result in sufferings arising from desires,
therefore cut them off at the root, as one would enemies disguised as friends.
Sensual pleasures are impermanent, deceptive by nature, empty, and causes of calamity; they are shared by many and should be shunned like venomous serpents. (Saundarananda 15.8)
Those things which, when sought, lead to suffering; when guarded, do not bring peace;
when lost, result in great grief; and even when obtained, do not bring satisfaction. (Saundarananda 15.9)
He who perceives satisfaction through the abundance of wealth, the fulfillment of purpose through the attainment of heaven,
and the arising of happiness from sensual desires, is ruined.
You ought not to remember here those sensual pleasures which are fleeting, unaccomplished, pithless, unstable, and pleasant only through mental construction.
If ill will or cruelty should disturb your mind, it must be cleared by its opposite, just as turbid water is clarified by a jewel. (Saundarananda 15.12)
The antidote to those two should be known as loving-kindness and compassion alone;
for there is a constant opposition between them, like that between light and darkness. (Saundarananda 15.13)
He whose misconduct has ceased but who still harbors malice,
destroys himself with his own dust, like an elephant after a bath.
For what noble person, possessed of compassion, would inflict further suffering upon mortals already afflicted by disease, death, old age, and the like? (Saundarananda 15.15)
Whether another person is harmed here by one's wicked mind or not,
the mind of that evil-hearted person is nonetheless consumed by fire immediately.
Therefore, toward all living beings, you ought to cultivate only loving-kindness and compassion;
you should not entertain thoughts of malice or violence.
Whatever a person habitually dwells upon as it presents itself, by that very thing his mind becomes inclined through practice. (Saundarananda 15.18)
Therefore, having abandoned what is unwholesome, you ought to meditate on the wholesome,
so that there may be for you benefit in this world and the attainment of the ultimate goal.
For unwholesome thoughts, once accumulated in the heart, grow ever stronger;
they produce harm equally for oneself and for others. (Saundarananda 15.20)
By creating obstacles to what is beneficial, they lead to one's own ruin;
but by destroying the state of being a worthy recipient, they lead to the ruin of another's devotion.
You should also practice non-distraction regarding mental actions;
however, O gentle one, you must never entertain unwholesome thoughts.
Whatever thought dwells in the mind for the sake of enjoying the three types of sensual pleasures,
one does not attain that quality [of pleasure], and it only serves to lead to bondage.
For the sake of harming sentient beings and for his own affliction, he falls into delusion and turbidity, and he proceeds toward hell. (Saundarananda 15.24)
You ought not to destroy yourself with unwholesome thoughts, like one digging the earth with his hands while clutching a fine sword adorned with jewels. (Saundarananda 15.25)
Just as one who is ignorant might burn freshly produced aloeswood as if it were common wood,
so too does one destroy this human state through unrighteousness.
Just as one might abandon a jewel for a clod of earth and carry it away from an island of jewels,
so too does one abandon the Dharma that leads to the highest bliss and contemplate the foul.
Just as one might go to the Himalayas and consume poison instead of medicine, so too, having attained human birth, one should practice evil and not what is auspicious. (Saundarananda 15.28)
Having understood that, you should dispel discursive thought through its opposite, just as one drives out a wedge from within a piece of wood with a finer wedge. (Saundarananda 15.29)

Furthermore, if there should arise anxiety regarding the prosperity or decline of one's kinsmen, the nature of the world of living beings must be examined in order to bring that anxiety to an end. (Saundarananda 15.30)
Among beings who are dragged through cyclic existence by their own karma, who is a stranger and who is a kinsman? It is only through delusion that one person becomes attached to another.
For in the past time, those who were strangers became your own kin;
and in the future time, those who are now strangers will become your own kin.
Just as birds gather here and there at evening, so too is the union of people with their own kin in birth after birth. (Saundarananda 15.33)
Just as travelers take refuge in various shelters on their journey and then depart, leaving them behind, so too is the meeting with kinsmen. (Saundarananda 15.34)
In this world, which is by nature divided, no one is dear to anyone;
the world is bound together by cause and effect, like a handful of sand.
"For the mother bears the son, thinking 'she will support me';
the son honors the mother, thinking 'she conceived me in her womb. (Saundarananda 15.36)
When kinsmen behave in a favorable manner toward their kin, they manifest affection; but in the opposite case, enmity arises. (Saundarananda 15.37)
A kinsman is seen as harmful, while a stranger is seen as beneficial; the world cuts off affection and creates it based on other circumstances. (Saundarananda 15.38)
Just as a painter might fall in love with a woman he himself has painted,
so too does one person, having created affection themselves, come together with another person.
Those kinsmen who were dear to you in the world beyond—what benefit do they provide for you now, or what benefit do you provide for them? (Saundarananda 15.40)
Therefore, having understood this through reflection, you ought not to entangle your mind [in worldly affairs];
for in saṃsāra there is no fixed distinction between one's own kin and other people.
If some such thought should arise in you, "That country is secure," "That one is well-supplied with food," or "That one is auspicious," (you should disregard it). Saundarananda 15.42.
O gentle one, having realized that the entire world is ablaze with those various fires of defects, you must abandon it; it must by no means be accepted. (Saundarananda 15.43)
And because of the turning of the wheel of the seasons, as well as hunger, thirst, and fatigue, suffering is constant everywhere; nowhere is there anything auspicious.
In some places there is cold, in some heat; in some places disease, and in others fear.
These afflict the world excessively; therefore, the world is without refuge.
Old age, disease, and death are the great terrors of this world;
there is no place where these terrors do not arise.
Wherever this body goes, suffering follows there;
there is no destination in the world where one who has gone is not afflicted.
Even a region that is delightful, well-supplied with food, and secure should be known as a "bad country" if one is tormented by afflictions there. (Saundarananda 15.48)
For this world, which is assailed by physical and mental sufferings,
there is no secure region anywhere where one who has gone there might be at ease.
When suffering exists everywhere, for everyone, and at all times, then, O gentle one, do not harbor desire or passion for these painted figures. (Saundarananda 15.50)
When your desire and passion for that have ceased,
then you will regard the entire world of the living as if it were ablaze.
Now, if some thought concerning death should arise within you,
it must be dispelled with effort, just as a disease located within one's own body is treated.
One should not place trust in life for even a moment;
for Time, like a lurking tiger, is the slayer of those who are heedless.
"It does not behove you to think, 'I am strong' or 'I am young';
for death slays in all conditions and takes no account of age. (Saundarananda 15.54)
For one who perceives the true goal and drags about this body— which is a field for misfortunes— neither hope for health nor hope for life arises.
Who could remain composed while carrying this body, which is the locus of the great elements, like a vessel for snakes that are mutually antagonistic? (Saundarananda 15.56)
This human being breathes out immediately after he breathes in;
understand that to be a marvel, for life is indeed not to be trusted. (Saundarananda 15.57)
This is another marvel: that one who has slept awakens, or having risen, sleeps again; for embodied beings have many enemies. (Saundarananda 15.58)
Who would place their trust in Death, who follows the world from the very moment of conception with the intent to destroy it, like an enemy with a raised weapon? (Saundarananda 15.59)
No man born in this world, however learned or powerful,
has ever conquered Death, nor is he conquering him now, nor will he ever conquer him.
For impetuous death, once it has arrived, cannot be warded off by conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, punishment, or restraint.
Therefore, you should not place your trust in this flickering life;
for Time constantly carries one away and does not wait for old age.
For one who perceives the world as essence-less, as fragile as a bubble upon water—
what person of sound mind would harbor thoughts of immortality?
Therefore, my friend, for the sake of abandoning these discursive thoughts, you ought to take mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation as your object in brief.
By this practice, you ought to cultivate at the proper time the antidotes to discursive thoughts, just as one applies medicines against diseases.

Just as a gold-washer, for the sake of gold, first discards the coarse dust and then discards even the fine particles for the sake of its purification, having cleansed them, he retains the fragments of gold. (Saundarananda 15.66)

With a mind disciplined for the sake of liberation, having first abandoned gross defects, he then abandons even the subtle ones for the sake of its purification; having purified the factors of the Dharma, he attains mastery.
Just as a smith here purifies gold that is covered by dross with water and intensely heats and repeatedly melts it in the fire,
so too does the practitioner of yoga here skillfully [purify] the mind that is obscured by defects.
Having purified it from the afflictions, he calms the mind and withdraws it.
And just as a goldsmith, by his own will, brings the gold— which is the basis for action— to a state of ease through various methods of ornamentation,
so too does a monk of pure mind bring that which is under his control even to the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
It calms the mind as it wishes and directs it wherever it desires.
