In the *Saundarananda*, the great poem, the fifteenth canto, titled "The Abandonment of Discursive Thought":

"Thus, by means of mental concentration, having gradually eliminated some things and cultivated others, the yogi, having attained the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), invariably acquires the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*). (Saund_16.1)
He possesses preeminent supernormal powers of many kinds, the comprehension of the mental conduct of others,
the long-term recollection of past births, and the divine, purified faculties of hearing and sight.
Beyond this, he applies his mind to the investigation of reality for the sake of the destruction of the outflows;
for from that, he correctly understands the four truths, beginning with suffering, as they truly are.
This suffering is of the nature of affliction; this is the cause of suffering, being of the nature of its origin;
this is the destruction of suffering, being of the nature of liberation; and this path leads to peace, being of the nature of protection.
Thus, having understood the noble truths with wisdom and having correctly penetrated them all four, one overcomes all taints through cultivation; having attained peace, one is not born again.

For because of the lack of understanding and lack of penetration regarding these four things whose nature is reality, the world, having mounted the swing of saṃsāra, goes from existence to existence and does not attain peace. (Saundarananda 16.6)
Therefore, understand that birth is, in brief, the root of calamities such as old age and the like, and is suffering itself;
for this birth is the field of all misfortunes, just as the earth is the source of all plants.
For that which is the birth of the embodied form with its sense faculties is the birth of manifold suffering;
and whatever is the arising of this physical frame is the very arising of death and disease. (Saundarananda 16.8)

Just as food mixed with poison, whether it be good or bad, leads to destruction and not to sustenance, so too in this world, every birth—whether among animals, above, or below—leads only to suffering and not to happiness. (Saundarananda 16.9)
When activity exists, the various misfortunes such as old age and the like prevail over living beings;
for even when violent winds are blowing, trees that have not yet sprouted do not sway.
Just as the wind has its source in space, as fire lies within the womb of the *śamī* tree,
and as water dwells within the earth, so too does suffering have its source in the body and the mind.

Just as fluidity is the inherent nature of water, solidity of the earth, motion of the wind, and constant heat of fire, so too is suffering the inherent nature of both the body and the mind. (Saundarananda 16.12)
When there is a body, there is the suffering of disease, old age, and so forth, as well as hunger, thirst, rain, heat, cold, and the like;
and when there is a mind dependent on form and accompanied by its continuations, there is the suffering of grief, discontent, anger, fear, and so on.
Having perceived the suffering of birth directly before you, know that suffering likewise exists in the past;
and just as that was suffering and this is suffering, know that suffering will likewise exist in the future. (Saundarananda 16.14)
For just as the nature of a seed is observed here to be such whether it has already sprouted or is yet to do so, it is likewise to be inferred;
and just as fire is perceived to be hot whether it has already been so or is yet to be so, it is indeed hot in both cases.

Therefore, O one of noble conduct, wherever the manifestation of name-and-form occurs in accordance with its qualities, there alone is suffering; for that which is liberated from it will not have suffering in the future, nor has it had it in the past, nor does it have it now.
And for that suffering of worldly involvement, the cause is the host of defects such as craving;
it is neither God, nor primordial nature, nor time, nor inherent essence, nor fate, nor chance.
And by this reason it should be understood that the world's engagement [with existence] is due to its defects;
for those possessed of passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*) die, but one who is free from passion and darkness is not born again. (Saundarananda 16.18)
When there is a particular desire, the employment of vehicles, seats, and so forth occurs in various instances;
therefore, it should be understood that the birth of living beings likewise occurs through the power of craving.

"Beholding beings who, under the sway of attachment, are exceedingly devoted to their own kind, know that these [afflictions] have been produced by those very defects through the power of habitual practice. (Saundarananda 16.20)
Just as a distinction arises here among the physical bases through anger, excessive joy, and so forth,
in that very same way, a distinction produced by the afflictions is not of a single form even across successive births.
In a birth where the [defilement of] hatred predominates, intense hatred arises; in one who is passionate, intense passion arises;
in one where delusion predominates, there is an excess of the power of delusion; and when those defilements are slight, the resulting defilement is likewise slight.
For just as one directly perceives the kind of fruit that is present, one understands the past seed from the arrival of that fruit;
and having directly understood the nature of the seed, one anticipates its future fruit. (Saundarananda 16.23)
In whichever births a person’s defects have been exhausted through detachment, he is not born again in those;
however, wherever a latent tendency toward defects remains, there that person is reborn against his will. (Saundarananda 16.24)

O gentle one, having understood that craving and the like are the causes of this manifold birth, cut them off if you desire liberation from suffering; for the cessation of effects results from the destruction of their causes.
Through the complete exhaustion of causes, realize for yourself the Dharma that is the cessation of suffering— peaceful, auspicious,
the fading away of craving, the shelter, the milkless, eternal, the protection, the unassailable, and the noble.
That state in which there is no birth, no old age, no death, no diseases, no union with the unpleasant,
and no separation from the beloved due to unfulfilled desires— that is the secure, ultimate, and immutable station.

Just as a lamp that has reached its extinction goes neither to the earth nor to the intermediate space, nor to any direction or intermediate point, but simply attains peace through the exhaustion of its oil; so too does he.
Thus, the one who has accomplished his task and attained liberation goes neither to the earth nor to the atmosphere;
he goes to no cardinal direction nor to any intermediate direction, but through the destruction of the afflictions, he attains absolute peace.
The means for its attainment is the path consisting of threefold wisdom and twofold tranquility;
that should be cultivated according to rule by the wise one, established in pure morality with its three gateways. (Saundarananda 16.30)

Right speech, along with right bodily action, and a livelihood that is pure according to the rule—these three, engaged in the practice of conduct, are based on ethical discipline (*śīla*) for the sake of embracing [wholesome] karma. (Saundarananda 16.31)
The noble vision regarding the truths such as suffering, right reflection, and exertion—
these three, when applied to the method of knowledge and based upon wisdom, lead to the complete destruction of the afflictions.
Through right method, right mindfulness and likewise right concentration are joined for the attainment of truth;
these two, engaged in the practice of yoga, provide a basis for tranquility in order to master the mind. *Saundarananda* 16.33.
Virtue does not allow the sprouts of afflictions to spread, just as the untimely season prevents the sprouts of seeds from growing;
for when a person’s virtue is pure, their faults cannot overcome them, just as modesty restrains the mind.
But concentration suppresses the afflictions, just as a mountain [stills] the torrents of great rivers;
for when concentration is established, the faults do not overpower one, like serpents bound by a mantra. (Saundarananda 16.35)
Wisdom, however, destroys the afflictions without exception, just as a mountain stream in the rainy season uproots the trees on its banks;
once burnt by it, the afflictions have no power to arise, just as trees cannot grow where they have been struck by a thunderbolt of fire. *Saundarananda 16.36*
Having thoroughly penetrated this noble eightfold path, which consists of three aggregates, is clear, unshakable, and sublime,
one abandons the causes of suffering and the faults, and attains that state of ultimate peace.
In its practice, there are steadfastness and straightforwardness, modesty and vigilance, and seclusion;
as well as fewness of desires, contentment, lack of attachment, a distaste for worldly activities, and forbearance. (Saundarananda 16.38)
He who understands suffering according to its true nature, as well as its origin and its cessation,
attains peace by means of the Noble Path while dwelling together with virtuous friends.
He who, being afflicted by disease, correctly understands the illness, its cause, and its remedy,
shall indeed attain health before long, being attended by wise friends.
Therefore, form the perception of a disease regarding the truth of suffering; likewise, form the perception of the cause of disease regarding its defects.
Form the perception of health regarding the truth of cessation, and the perception of medicine regarding the truth of the path.
Therefore, understand that activity is suffering, and recognize the defects that cause it to proceed;
attain cessation, and likewise understand the path that brings about that cessation.
Therefore, while your head and your garment are ablaze, you must direct your mind toward the realization of truth;
for if one does not perceive the true method, the world has already been burnt, is being burnt now, and will continue to be burnt.

Whenever one perceives that name-and-form is subject to decay, that vision of his is correct; and through that correct vision, he attains disenchantment, and because of the destruction of delight, his passion comes to an end. (Saundarananda 16.44)
And through the destruction of both delight and passion, I declare the mind to be perfectly liberated;
with that perfect liberation of the mind from those two, there is nothing further for it to be done.
For one who understands name-and-form according to their own nature, as well as its cause and its cessation, and who truly sees this, I declare that there is the complete destruction of the outflows.
Therefore, my dear friend, having exerted supreme vigor, strive quickly for the destruction of the outflows;
specifically examining the elements as suffering, impermanent, and selfless.

For he who understands the six elements—earth, water, fire, and the rest—both in their general nature and by their own specific characteristics, and understands nothing other than them, understands the ultimate liberation from them. (Saundarananda 16.48)
Furthermore, one who is determined to abandon the afflictions must examine both the proper time and the appropriate means;
for even spiritual practice, when performed at the wrong time or by the wrong means, leads to harm rather than to its intended virtue.
If one were to milk a cow whose calf has not yet been born, that untimely milking would yield no milk at all;
or even if it were the proper time, one would obtain no milk if, out of delusion, one were to milk the cow from its horn.
One who desires fire will not obtain it from wet wood even with great effort;
nor does one obtain fire from dry wood by merely throwing it down, if the proper means are lacking. (Saundarananda 16.51)
Having duly examined the place and time, as well as the measure and the means for yoga,
and having carefully considered one's own strength and weakness, one should apply effort that is not contrary to those factors.
That sign which was described as "grasping" when the heart is burning should not be cultivated;
for in this way the mind does not attain tranquility, just as fire is not extinguished by being fanned. (Saundarananda 16.53)
When the mind has become agitated, that is the time for whatever cause is certain to lead to its pacification;
for in this way the mind attains tranquility, just as a blazing fire is extinguished by water. (Saundarananda 16.54)
That cause which is certain to bring about tranquility should not be cultivated when the mind is already sinking;
for in this way the mind sinks even further, like a fire of little substance that is not fanned.
When the mind has fallen into lethargy, that which is a fixed, uplifting sign is the appropriate time [to apply it];
for in this way the mind becomes capable of action, like a fire that is dying down when fed with fuel. (Saundarananda 16.56)
Nor is a state of equanimity desired when the mind has fallen into lethargy or is agitated;
for if it is neglected in such a state, it will produce intense harm, like an untreated disease in a patient. (Saundarananda 16.57)
When the mind has attained equanimity, that is the time for the sign fixed upon equanimity;
for in this way, the application becomes effective for its task, like a chariot drawn by well-trained horses.
Even when the mind is agitated by the fire of passion, the practice of cultivating loving-kindness should not be performed;
for one whose nature is dominated by passion becomes deluded by loving-kindness, just as one suffering from a phlegm disorder is further confounded by consuming oily food.
When the mind is agitated by passion, one should attain steadfastness and cultivate the sign of the foul;
for one whose nature is dominated by passion thus attains peace, just as one whose nature is dominated by phlegm finds relief by consuming something dry.
When the fault of malice has arisen in the mind, one must not cultivate an unwholesome object;
for to one whose nature is hatred, the unwholesome leads to ruin, just as a cooling treatment is fatal to one whose nature is dominated by bile.
But when the mind is agitated by the fault of malice, one should cultivate loving-kindness by removing its opposing factors;
for loving-kindness serves to pacify one whose nature is hatred, just as cooling treatments serve one whose nature is bilious heat.
When the movement of the mind is bound by delusion, both loving-kindness and the meditation on the foul become ineffective;
for through those two, one falls into further confusion, as if being struck by something harsh and airy in nature.
When the activity of the mind is characterized by delusion, one should cultivate the dwelling upon the nature of things as they truly are;
for when the mind is bewildered, this is the path to peace, just as an unctuous treatment is for a wind-natured disorder.

For just as a goldsmith here blows upon that gold at the proper time with a bellows, at the proper time sprinkles it with water, and in due course at the proper time remains indifferent to it; ||| Saund_16.65 |||
For one smelting gold might burn it if one blows at the wrong time; one might extinguish it by casting it into water at the wrong time;
nor indeed would one bring it to perfect maturity by neglecting it at the wrong time.

One must correctly observe with the mind the proper signs for exertion, for tranquility, and likewise for equanimity at the appropriate time; for even effort is destroyed if it is not preceded by the right means.
Thus the Sugata spoke to him of the turning away from what is improper and of what is proper;
and further, having understood his various conduct, he taught the methods for the abandonment of discursive thought.
Just as a physician applies a remedy for the pacification of whichever humor— bile, phlegm, or wind— has become provoked, so too did the Buddha act regarding the defilements.

If one does not destroy unwholesome thoughts through a single eon because they have become so thoroughly habitual, then one should begin a second method; for a virtuous practitioner should never abandon their application.
Because the multitude of afflictions has been accumulated since beginningless time and is thus powerful,
and because correct application is difficult to achieve, these faults cannot indeed be severed all at once.
Just as one skilled man drives out a large nail with another nail, so too should one cast away that very same unwholesome sign by resorting to a different sign. (Saundarananda 16.72)

Nevertheless, if unwholesome thought does not subside because it has not yet been mastered through internal self-reflection, it must be abandoned by examining its faults, just as a traveler avoids a path infested with wild beasts. (Saundarananda 16.73)

Just as one afflicted by hunger, desiring to live, does not wish to eat food mixed with poison, even so the wise man, knowing it to be fraught with faults, abandons an inauspicious sign. (Saundarananda 16.74)
For who is able to restrain him who does not perceive a fault as a fault? And he who perceives virtue in virtue proceeds toward it even when being restrained. (Saundarananda 16.75)
For those born of noble lineage feel ashamed when unwholesome deeds manifest in public;
just as a wise, handsome youth feels abashed when foul, impure, and unseen things cling to his throat.
But if unwholesome thoughts should persist even in the slightest degree despite being shaken off,
one should employ other activities, such as the practice of study, as a method to cause them to be forgotten.
Even if one must sleep, the wise person should do so, or even endure physical exhaustion;
but one should never intentionally contemplate an improper object, for by being attached to it, misfortune arises.

Just as one who is terrified of thieves at night would not wish to open his door even to loved ones, so the wise man withdraws his application from faults, whether they be good or bad. (Saundarananda 16.79)
If, even when being restrained by such means as these, they do not turn away,
then they should be eliminated like defects in gold by removing what is coarsest.
Just as a man, weary of the sharp application of sensual desires beginning with rapid journeys,
seeks refuge [in tranquility], even so should the wise person conduct themselves regarding the faults [of the senses].
If those unwholesome thoughts do not subside because their antidotes have not been attained,
they must not be tolerated for even a moment, like serpents in one's house that remain unchecked.

Even by pressing tooth against tooth, or even by pressing the tip of the palate with the tongue, and by firmly grasping the mind with the mind, you must exert effort; yet they will not remain under your control.
What is surprising here, if one who is free from delusion, having gone to the forest with a tranquil mind, should not be bewildered?
He who, though being assailed in his heart by the causes of that [delusion], is not shaken—he is the one who has accomplished his task, he is the steadfast man.
Therefore, first purify the path for the realization of the Noble Truths by this method,
just as a king who has set out on an expedition desires to conquer unconquered fortune in order to subdue his enemies.
These auspicious forests all around are conducive to yoga and untouched by the noise of people;
having ensured mere physical seclusion, devote yourself to the path for the abandonment of the afflictions.
Kauṇḍinya, Nanda, Kṛmila, and Aniruddha; Tiṣya and Upasena, Vimala, and Rādha; Bāṣpa and Uttara, Dhautaki and Moharāja; Kātyāyana, Dravya, Pininda, and Vatsa.
Bhaddāli, Bhadrāyaṇa, Sarpadāsa, Subhūti, Godatta, Sujāta, Vatsa,
Saṃgrāmajit, Bhadrajit, Aśvajit, Śroṇa, Śoṇa, and Koṭikarṇa.
Kṣema, Ājita, Nandana, Nanda, Mātṛ, Upāli, Vāgīśa, Yaśas, Yaśodā,
Mahāhvaya, Valkalin, Rāṣṭrapāla, Sudarśana, Svāgata, and Meghika.
He was Kapphiṇa, Kāśyapa, Auruvelva, Mahā-Kāśyapa, Tiṣya, and Nanda;
Pūrṇa, Pūrṇa, and that Pūrṇaka, as well as Śoṇāparānta—that very Pūrṇa.
Śāradvatīputra, Subāhu, Cunda, Kondeya, Kāpya, Bhṛgu, Kuṇṭha, Dhāna,
along with Śaivala, the two Revata and Kauṣṭhila, he of the Maudgalya clan, and Gavāmpati.
Perform quickly and according to the rule that very same exertion which they practiced in the practice of yoga;
then you will surely attain the state reached by them, as well as renown enveloped in happiness. (Saundarananda 16.92)
Just as a substance may be pungent in taste yet sweet when consumed in its digestion,
so too is his vigor pungent through exertion, yet its ripening is sweet for the accomplishment of his goal.
For energy is the supreme root in the accomplishment of what is to be done; without energy, there is no success whatsoever.
From energy arises every perfection here in this world, while the absence of energy is total evil.
The failure to obtain what has not been obtained, the certain loss of what has already been obtained, self-contempt, wretchedness, being humiliated by superiors,
darkness, lack of luster, and the cessation of learning, discipline, and contentment.
For men who lack vigor, there occurs downfall and ruin.
Having heard this method, he is unable to attain further growth;
having known the supreme Dharma, he is unable to dwell upon it;
and having abandoned the home for liberation, he is unable to attain peace.
In this matter, the cause of a man's failure is laziness; it is not an external enemy.
If one digs the earth with undiminished zeal, one finds water;
by continuously churning the two fire-sticks, one produces fire.
Indeed, those who apply themselves to yoga certainly obtain the fruit of their exertion.
For rivers, flowing swiftly and constantly, even pierce through mountains.
Having ploughed the earth and protected the cattle through hundreds of labors, one reaps the excellence of the harvest;
having diligently plunged into the waters of the ocean, one sports with the splendor of jewels;
and having struck down the prowess of enemies with arrows, one enjoys the sovereignty of a lord of men.
Therefore, apply that energy toward tranquility; for when energy is disciplined, all prosperities follow.
The sixteenth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Noble Truths," in the epic poem *Saundarananda*.

Then Nanda, having been thus instructed in the path of reality and having attained the path to liberation, bowed with his whole being to the Teacher and went to the forest to abandon the afflictions. *Saundarananda* 17.1.
There he saw a clearing with soft, dark-green grass, peaceful and surrounded by groves of trees, embraced by a silent river flowing with water as blue as lapis lazuli.
Having performed the purification of his feet there at the base of a pure, auspicious, and glorious tree,
he bound his loincloth for the sake of liberation and assumed the cross-legged posture, resting it firmly upon his lap.

Having set his body straight and composed, having established mindfulness directed toward the body, and having withdrawn all his senses within himself, he applied himself with diligence to that yoga. *Saundarananda 17.4*
Then, desiring to realize the entirety of reality and wishing to perform the practices conducive to liberation,
he proceeded upon the ground for the cultivation of the mind through worldly knowledge and tranquility.

Having summoned fortitude, applied energy, cast off attachment, and grasped his own power, he became tranquil in mind, established in self-restraint, and at ease; thus, he was no longer concerned with sense objects.

Even though his intellect was disciplined and his mind was directed toward renunciation, the notion of sensual desire caused his mind to become agitated due to long-standing habituation, like lightning striking water during the rainy season.
Recognizing that it was a state of obsessive passion, the wise man immediately cast aside that which caused an obstacle to the Dharma,
just as a self-controlled man, his mind overwhelmed by anger, casts off even a beloved woman whose virtues have become excessive.
But for him who had exerted vigor in order to pacify the mind, an unwholesome thought arose once more, like a terrible affliction befalling one intent on destroying a disease. (Saundarananda 17.9)

To counteract that [obstacle], he resorted to another virtuous means conducive to yoga, like a man whose strength is exhausted and who is being driven out by a powerful enemy seeking a place of refuge. (Saundarananda 17.10)

Just as a king, having established his city, applied his rod of punishment, won over his friends, and subdued his enemies, attains previously unattained land—such indeed is the policy for one seeking liberation as well. (Saundarananda 17.11)

For even for the yogin who desires liberation, the mind is his city, the method of knowledge is his staff, virtues are his friends, and faults are his enemies; he strives for that purpose which is liberation.
Desirous of escaping from the great web of suffering and seeking to enter upon the attainment of the path to liberation,
he went toward tranquility with his vision somewhat gained, wishing to behold the supreme Noble Path.
He who is homeless though he has a dwelling in darkness, even after hearing the truth, would remain heedless;
but since he was a fit vessel for liberation, he withdrew his mind within his own self. (Saundarananda 17.14)

Then the self-possessed one duly conducted an investigation into phenomena according to their equipment, conditions, intrinsic nature, gratification, specific defects, and likewise their nature as an escape. (Saundarananda 17.15)
Desiring to see the essence of both the material and the immaterial, he scrutinized the body;
then he scrutinized the body as indeed impure, suffering, impermanent, non-self, and devoid of a self. (Saundarananda 17.16)
For by means of that preeminent worldly path, through [the contemplations of] impermanence, emptiness, selflessness, and suffering, he caused the tree of the afflictions to tremble.
Because everything here comes into being after not having been, and having come into being, necessarily ceases to exist again;
and because it is produced together with its cause and possesses a perishable cause, he thus discerned that the world is impermanent.
Since for one who is born, the engagement with action— which is the cause of bondage and the destruction [of liberation]—
is inevitably entailed in that which is called "pleasure" (only) as a means of counteracting suffering, he therefore perceived worldly existence to be suffering.
And since that which arises from the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) is solitary, with no agent whatsoever nor any experiencer,
but rather proceeds from the conjunction [of conditions], he therefore beheld this world as empty.

Because the world is devoid of effort and lacks independence, and no single being exercises sovereignty over its actions, and because entities arise in dependence upon this or that [condition], he realized the world to be without self. (Saundarananda 17.21)

Then, like one fanning for wind on a hot day, or producing fire from wood by friction, or digging for water within the earth, he attained that world-surpassing, difficult-to-reach path. (Saundarananda 17.22)
Having strung the bow of right knowledge and donned the armor of mindfulness, standing upon the vehicle of pure ethical discipline and vows,
he stood ready for victory, desiring to fight against the enemies of the afflictions stationed on the battlefield of the mind.
Then, having taken up the sharp weapons of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and mounted upon the supreme vehicle of the right efforts (samyakpradhāna),
he gradually plunged into the army of the afflictions (kleśa) with a force consisting of the elephants that are the factors of the path (mārgāṅga).

With arrows consisting of the applications of mindfulness, he instantly shattered his enemies— the four causes of suffering— which consist of the perversions, by means of their respective four bases of activity.
With the five peerless powers of the noble ones, he shattered the five mental barrennesses;
likewise, with the eight noble paths, he utterly routed the eight elephants of false views.
Then, having shaken off every view of a self and being one who speaks no more of worldly discourse regarding the Four Truths, he—
possessing pure conduct, vows, and vision of the Dharma— attained the first stage of the fruit of the Dharma.

Through the vision of the four noble truths and through the dissociation from a portion of the afflictions, and also through the attainment of individual excellence and the direct perception of the bliss of the wise, [he is liberated]. (Saundarananda 17.28)
Due to the firmness of his serene confidence, the stability of his fortitude, his lack of delusion regarding the Four Truths,
and the flawlessness of his supreme ethical conduct, he became free from doubt concerning the Dharma-method.
Freed from the net of false views and beholding the world as it truly is,
he attained a joy rooted in knowledge and experienced even greater clarity toward his teacher.
He who understands that the process of existence is determined, arising neither from another cause nor without a cause;
he who perceives each specific thing as it occurs in dependence upon its respective conditions—he beholds the ultimate Dharma.
Furthermore, he gazes upon the Buddha, the supreme among the Noble Ones, the teacher of that Dharma, who has attained the eye of wisdom.
Just as a healthy man, freed from disease by the instruction of Śiva,
gratefully remembers the physician and beholds him with the vision of his mind, so too is he satisfied through loving-kindness and his knowledge of the scriptures.

Liberated by the noble path, the Tathāgata, who knows reality and possesses the noble truth, beholds [the world] while recollecting it; as a bodily witness, he is satisfied by loving-kindness and by omniscience.

Released from destructive views and having seen the end of renewed existence, he cast aside his aversion toward the manifestations of the afflictions; he feared neither death nor the miserable realms.
Filled with a collection of impurities— skin, sinews, fat, marrow, blood, bone, flesh, hair, and so forth—
he, observing that body, reflected upon its essence and did not find even an atom of it.
Firm in soul, he thinned out both sensual desire and aversion by that very yoga;
having made those two thin on his broad-chested body, he attained the second fruit in the noble Dharma.

With the weapons of yoga and the arrows of the foul, he shattered the bow of greed, the arrow of conceptualization, and the great enemy passion— which remained but a small remnant— by means of those [arrows] which had realized the true nature of the body.
He struck down that enemy— ill-will— which has hatred as its weapon, anger as its scattered arrows, and malice as its internal offspring—
with arrows of loving-kindness stored in the quiver of fortitude and released from the bowstring of patience.
Then the Hero cut away the three roots of that impure one by means of the three bases of liberation,
just as an enemy with three iron-tipped arrows might strike down three foes standing at the head of an army, holding their bows.
Having overcome those enemies who held him back from transcending the realm of desire,
he attained the fruit of non-returning through spiritual practice and stood like a gateway to the city of Nirvāṇa.

Then he attained the first dhyāna, which is secluded from sensual desires and from impure states, accompanied by directed thought and sustained investigation, and endowed with the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
Released from the torment of the fire of desire, he attained supreme joy from the bliss of meditation;
like one exhausted by heat plunging into water, or like a pauper obtaining vast wealth.

There too, having recognized that the discursive thoughts directed toward those objects and the reflections flowing toward their merits and defects were unpeaceful and agitating to the mind, he resolved to be free from them.
Just as waves cause agitation in the ocean that carries deep and tranquil waters,
so too do discursive thoughts, acting like waves, cause agitation in the water of the mind when it has become one-pointed.
Just as sounds cause distress to one who is weary, asleep, or at rest,
so do discursive thoughts cause affliction to one who has attained internal one-pointedness.
Then, through the one-pointedness of his mind, he meditated upon that second dhyāna— tranquil, free from applied thought and sustained reflection,
born of concentration, and consisting of the joy and happiness of inner peace.
Having attained that meditative absorption, he achieved mental silence and experienced a supreme joy never before obtained;
yet, even regarding that joy, he perceived its defects in the very same way as he had done toward discursive thoughts.
For wherever one has supreme delight in an object, there is indeed suffering for him through its reversal;
therefore, perceiving the defects therein, he ascended to the yoga of the waning of delight.

Then, experiencing with his body that bliss which is free from passion and cherished by the noble ones, he dwelt mindful and clearly conscious; having attained the third dhyāna, the steadfast one remained as one who is equanimous.
Because there is no happiness beyond that, and no further progression of happiness surpassing it,
he who knows the higher and the lower spoke of the stage of the Śubhakṛtsnas as "supreme" through his loving-kindness.
Even in that meditative absorption, he then perceived a fault; he considered the supreme state to be peaceful and indeed immovable.
Yet his mind, constantly engaged in the experience of pleasure as it arose, was still stirred by mental effort.
Where there is agitation, there is vibration; and where there is vibration, there is suffering.
Therefore, because it is characterized by agitation, ascetics who desire tranquility abandon that which is called "pleasure."
Then, through the prior abandonment of both pleasure and pain as well as mental fluctuation,
he attained the fourth dhyāna, which is pure, characterized by equanimity and mindfulness, and is neither painful nor pleasant.
But because in that [fourth dhyāna] there is neither pleasure nor pain, and because knowledge exists therein operating upon its object,
therefore "purity of equanimity and mindfulness" is defined in the procedure for the fourth dhyāna.
Relying upon that fourth dhyāna, he then set his mind toward the attainment of arhatship,
just as a king, relying on a powerful and noble ally, desires to conquer unconquered territories.
Then, impelled by his cultivation of wisdom, he completely severed with the sword of insight those five higher fetters,
the supreme bonds, the supreme fetters that lead upward.
With the seven nāgas that are the factors of enlightenment, he crushed those very seven latent tendencies of the mind,
just as Time, with its seven planets, destroys the seven continents when their destruction is imminent.

For Nanda applied to the faults that same mode of behavior which fire, trees, clarified butter, and water maintain toward a water-vessel, wind, fire, and the sun— by means of extinguishing, uprooting, burning, and drying.

Thus, with a raft possessing eight components, he crossed over the difficult-to-traverse ocean of suffering—possessing three currents, three crocodiles, three waves, a single body of water, five speeds, two shores, and two sharks. *Saundarananda* 17.60.
Having attained arhatship, he became worthy of honor—free from longing, free from craving, and free from hope;
fearless, sorrowless, devoid of pride, and dispassionate, he appeared as if transformed by his steadfastness.
Then, through that instruction of his brother and teacher, and by his own prowess, Nanda—with a tranquil mind and his purpose fully accomplished—spoke these words to himself: *Saundarananda 17.62*
Homage be to that Sugata, who, desiring my welfare and possessing a compassionate nature,
has turned back many sufferings for me and brought forth abundant happiness.
For I, being dragged along the path consisting of suffering by ignoble passion born of the body,
have been turned back by the goad of his words, like a proud elephant by a hook.

"By the command of that compassionate Teacher, having indeed uprooted the thorn of passion residing in my heart, even now I experience such great happiness; how much more so, then, when all [defilements] are destroyed and I am at peace! (Saundarananda 17.65)

For, having extinguished the blazing fire of desire with the water of fortitude as one extinguishes a fire with water, I have now attained supreme refreshment, like one who has descended into a cool lake after the summer heat.
Nothing is dear to me, nor is anything undear; I have no attachment, so how could there be aversion?
Because of the absence of both, I am immediately happy, like one released from cold and heat.
As one who has found safety after great terror, as one who has attained liberation from a vast prison,
as one without a boat who has reached the further shore of the great ocean, and as one who has come upon light after a terrifying darkness.
It was like regaining health from an unbearable disease, like freedom from debt after an infinite number of obligations,
like escaping from the presence of enemies, and like obtaining a bountiful harvest through the application of diligent effort.
In the same way, I have attained supreme peace through the power of that Vināyaka;
once again, I offer salutation after salutation to this Arhat, the Tathāgata. (Saundarananda 17.70)

By whom I was led to the golden-peaked mountain and shown heaven by means of the example of the female monkeys—there, my soul consumed by desire, I was dragged away by celestial women and plunged into an age consisting entirely of young women. (Saundarananda 17.71)
And having been drawn out from that mire of calamity and misfortune— like an elephant slowly emerging from the mud—
you are now liberated in this peaceful, stainless, feverless, sorrowless, and ultimate True Dharma, which is free from darkness.

I bow my head to that Great Seer, the supremely compassionate one, who knows the nature of qualities and knows the intentions [of beings]; to the Perfectly Awakened One, possessed of the ten powers, the foremost of physicians, the savior—to him I bow once again. (Saundarananda 17.73)

In the epic poem *Saundarananda*, this is the seventeenth canto, titled "The Attainment of the Immortal. Then Nanda, having achieved his purpose, approached his teacher like a twice-born youth who has mastered the Vedas, like a merchant who has swiftly obtained great profit, or like a king who has conquered an enemy army. *Saundarananda* 18.1.
For at the time of the completion of his knowledge, it is pleasant for a disciple to see his teacher, and likewise for a teacher to see his disciple;
since he desired to see the Sage, [the king thought], "Your exertion toward me has indeed borne fruit."
For it is right that one who has attained a distinction should offer honor upon the head of the one by whom it was achieved;
thus, even a noble one still possessed of passion acts out of gratitude—how much more so one whose pride is destroyed and who is free from passion?
For one whose devotion arises from wealth and desire, that devotion remains with its roots firmly established;
but for one whose passion for devotion follows from the path of Dharma, his grace penetrates deep into the heart.
Clad in saffron robes and radiant as gold, he then bowed his head to the Guru,
like a *karṇikāra* tree with the copper-red glow of its young shoots stirred by the wind and the brilliant beauty of its flowers.

Then, for the purpose of demonstrating his own qualities as a disciple, the qualities of the Great Sage as a teacher, and [the excellence of the task], he recounted the accomplishment of his mission, not out of pride. (Saundarananda 18.6)

O Lord, that extremely sharp dart of views which had plunged deep into my heart and tormented me intensely has been extracted by the pincers of your words, like a splinter removed by one skilled in extracting splinters.

I had fallen into a state of doubt, but that uncertainty has been severed by you; O one free from doubt, through your teaching I have come to the true path, like one who had lost his way finding a good guide.
That poison of Kandarpa which I drank through my senses, driven by passion and pride,
has been destroyed by the medicinal herb of your words, just as a deadly poison is neutralized by a great antidote.
Birth has come to an end; O you who have cast off birth, I have dwelt perfectly in the practice of the true Dharma.
Everything that was to be done has been done by me; O you who have accomplished your task, I am one who exists in the worlds, yet I am not subject to worldly conditions.

Having well drunk from your cow—whose udders are loving-kindness, whose beautiful dewlap is the secondary marks, whose milk is the true Dharma, and whose horns are eloquence—I am satisfied, like a thirsty calf of noble color drinking from a cow. (Saundarananda 18.11)
O Sage, understand briefly from me this realization which has come to me as I see;
O Omniscient One, although this is surely known to you, I wish to speak of my own personal practice. (Saundarananda 18.12)

For other virtuous people who desire liberation, having heard the method for liberation from another, strive happily by that very path, just as those afflicted by disease do after hearing of one who has been freed from disease. (Saundarananda 18.13)
In this birth, I know the earth and other elements as the constituent parts [of the body], but I do not perceive any "self" within those elements such as earth.
Therefore, I have no attachment to them; my mind regards what is outside the body as equal to it. (Saundarananda 18.14)
Since I perceive the five aggregates, beginning with form, to be flickering and devoid of essence,
and indeed to be without self and murderous in nature, I am therefore liberated from these inauspicious things.

Since I perceive the arising and passing away of the sense faculties in all their states, I have no attachment even toward them, for they are impermanent, selfless, and suffering. (Saundarananda 18.16)

Since I see the world as established in birth, devoid of essence, and entirely unreal, my mind is thus bound by my intellect; there is no longer any agitation in me by which [the world] might be moved.
Since I am unattached to the diversity of food amidst these fourfold and manifold attachments—
neither infatuated nor bound by it— I am therefore liberated from those three states of existence.

Since I am independent and my mind is unattached to the phenomena of worldly convention— such as what is seen and heard— and since I have attained equanimity therein, I have reached dissociation and am liberated.
Having spoken thus, out of profound reverence for his teacher, he prostrated himself upon the earth with his entire body;
anointed with red sandalwood, he appeared like a great golden pillar set in motion.

Then, having heard of his former steadfastness and his prophetic declaration, as well as his serene faith following from the sequence of the Dharma, the Sage, whose voice was like the sound of a thundercloud, addressed him who had previously strayed through negligence: *Saundarananda 18.21*
Arise, you who are established in the Dharma cherished by disciples! Why have you fallen at my feet with your head?
To me, prostration is not such an act of worship as this very practice of the Dharma.
Today you have truly gone forth as a renunciant, O self-conqueror, by whom sovereignty over the self has been attained;
for the life of renunciation is excellent for one who has conquered the self, but not for one of fickle mind whose senses are unsubdued.
Today you are endowed with supreme purity, since your speech, body, and mind are pure;
therefore, O gentle one, you shall not again behold the unclean and unpleasant bed of the womb.

Today your learning has become meaningful; having practiced the Dharma in accordance with what you have heard, one who has mastered the scriptures yet acts contrary to them is indeed to be censured, like a powerless man grasping a weapon.
"Oh, how steadfast is your resolve, you whose nature is beyond the sensory realm, that you have set your mind upon the method for liberation!
For it is only the fool who, in this world, succumbs to terror at the destruction of birth, thinking, 'I shall meet my end.'"

By good fortune, this rare convergence of conditions has not been rendered fruitless through the power of delusion; for once it has passed away, it arises again only with great difficulty, like a turtle encountering the hole of a yoke in the ocean. (Saundarananda 18.27)
Having conquered Māra, who is difficult to restrain in battle, you are today a hero at the head of the fray in this world;
for even one who is brave should be known as no hero if he is struck down by faults, just as an enemy is slain. *Saundarananda* 18.28.
Having extinguished the blazing fire of passion, you are today a hero at the head of the battle in this world;
for even on a noble bed, one whose mind is consumed by the fire of the afflictions (*kleśa*) sleeps in misery.
Formerly you were exalted by the intoxication of wealth, but today you are truly prosperous through the cessation of craving.
For as long as a person in this world possesses craving, they are always poor, even if they are fully endowed with prosperity.
"It is now fitting for you to declare, 'King Śuddhodana is my father';
for when one has fallen from the Dharma due to the downfall brought about by one's ancestors, a claim of noble lineage is indeed not to be praised."
By good fortune you have attained supreme peace, like one who has reached the essence after crossing a wilderness;
for everyone caught in the cycle of existence is afflicted by fear, just as one who has entered a wilderness.
"When shall I see Nanda, dwelling in the forest, subsisting on alms, disciplined, and composed?
Such was my desire to behold you from the very beginning; thus it is by good fortune that you have now become visible to me.
For even one who is formless may be beautiful when well-adorned with his own most excellent virtues;
but one who is overwhelmed by defiling faults is truly ugly, even if he be handsome to behold.
Today your wisdom has been proven supreme, by which you have accomplished your entire purpose;
for even one exalted by learning lacks wisdom if his intellect does not arise toward the highest good. (Saundarananda 18.35)
Even among people with eyes wide open, the eye of one who lacks the eye consisting of wisdom remains as if closed; for even though he possesses physical sight, he has no true vision.

Afflicted by suffering, the world undergoes exhaustion through agriculture and other labors for the sake of remedying that pain; yet that suffering returns incessantly and even increases—today, however, its end has been brought about by you through knowledge.

"The world indeed proceeds with the thought, 'May there be no suffering for me; may there be only happiness for me,' yet it does not know how that [happiness] might truly come to pass, as difficult as it is to obtain, which has now been attained by you. (Saundarananda 18.38)

Having been addressed thus for his welfare by the Tathāgata, Nanda—his intellect and mind now firm, indifferent to praise and blame, and with palms joined in reverence—spoke these words: (Saundarananda 18.39).

Oh! O Seer of Distinctions, you have shown me this exceptional compassion, in that I, O Blessed One, though submerged in the mire of desire, have been rescued from the fear of saṃsāra against my will.

If I had not been rescued by you, my brother, who are a guide to the highest good; by my father, who abides in the fruit [of his own practice]; and likewise by my mother—then, fallen from the caravan, I would have perished like one who has failed to achieve his purpose.
For one who is peaceful and contented, solitude is happiness; for the examiner who has realized reality, it is happiness;
and for one whose pride is abandoned and who is free from intoxication, freedom from passion is the happiness of one whose mind is unattached.

Therefore, having thoroughly understood reality, having completely shaken off faults, and having attained peace, I now contemplate my own refuge; I think no more of that person, nor of the apsarases, nor of the gods.
For having tasted this pure happiness born of tranquility, my mind no longer desires the pleasure born of passion;
it is like the nectar of the gods to one who has already eaten a most costly meal that was not brought by the deities. (Saundarananda 18.44)
Alas! The world, blinded by ignorant consciousness, does not perceive the supreme bliss within the inner self;
for, having cast aside the profound happiness of the inner self, it indeed pursues the toil for the sake of sensual pleasure.
For just as a foolish person, having come to a mine of jewels, might discard the jewels and carry away worthless stones;
so too, having cast aside the supreme bliss of perfect awakening, one would undergo toil for the sake of attaining the pleasure of sensual desires. (Saundarananda 18.46)
Oh, how supreme is the Tathāgata’s desire to favor sentient beings, for his mind is so exceedingly compassionate!
O Sage, casting aside the highest bliss of meditative absorption, you exert yourself for the sake of bringing an end to the suffering of others.
I am unable to repay you today, my compassionate teacher who desires my welfare,
by whom I was rescued from the ocean of existence as one whose ship has been shattered by the waves of the great sea.

Then the Sage, the unsurpassed among speakers, having heard his reasoned words which indicated that all outflows were abandoned, spoke this, which only the Blessed One himself is worthy to utter: *Saundarananda 18.49*
O wise one, you alone, having accomplished your purpose and knowing the ultimate truth, are worthy to speak this;
like a great merchant who has crossed the wilderness and obtained his goal, you have fulfilled the task for your excellent guide.

Just as an accomplished Arhat whose mind is stilled perceives the Buddha, the caravan leader for those to be tamed by men, even one who has seen the Truth does not understand him in that same way; how much less, then, can an ordinary person, even if he were possessed of intelligence?
This gratitude of yours is truly worthy of you, whose mind is entirely liberated from passion and darkness;
for in a world established in the preponderance of passion, O grateful one, the state of being grateful is indeed rare to find.
Therefore, I have much more that I wish to say to you; for you, being humble and devoted, deserve my command.
"You have accomplished your task and reached the supreme goal; there is not even the slightest thing remaining for you to do.
Therefore, O gentle one, from this point forward, move about out of compassion, liberating others who have fallen into distress. (Saundarananda 18.54)

The base man undertakes action here for the sake of this world alone; the mediocre man, however, performs action pertaining to both worlds; the middling man acts for the sake of fruit in the world beyond; but the one of distinguished dharma acts, moreover, so as not to engage in rebirth at all.

But among these, he is considered even more excellent than the most excellent who, having attained the supreme and final Dharma, desires to teach tranquility to others without regard for the personal exertion it entails. (Saundarananda 18.56)
Therefore, O steadfast one, setting aside your own task here, attend now to the task of others as well;
while sentient beings wander with their minds shrouded in darkness, let this lamp of sacred learning be held aloft in the night. (Saundarananda 18.57)

Let the astonished people in the city say, while you stand there delivering teachings on the Dharma: "Oh, how wonderful! Even this one who was once full of passion now delivers discourse for the sake of liberation! (Saundarananda 18.58)
For having firmly promised you, her mind is surely steady, with its various desires for sense-objects turned away;
that bride in your home, emulating you, will also make stories regarding women full of dispassion.
When you have become established in supreme fortitude and fixed in the truth, she will certainly no longer find delight in the household life—
just as the discerning man’s mind, when the internal self is secluded through tranquility and self-restraint, finds no pleasure in sensual pleasures.
Thus, having bowed his head and simultaneously grasped both the words and the feet of the Teacher— the Arhat, the supremely compassionate—
he departed from the side of the Sage, healthy, with a tranquil heart, his task accomplished, like an elephant freed from its rut.

At the proper time, he entered the city for alms, captivating the eyes of the people; equal toward gain and loss, pleasure and pain, and other such things, his senses composed and free from desire, he delivered a discourse on liberation to those who sought it at that moment. He did not disparage others who had gone astray, nor did he exalt himself. (Saundarananda 18.62)

Thus, this work, containing the essence of liberation for the sake of tranquility rather than mere pleasure, has been composed by means of the artifice of poetry in order to capture the attention of those whose minds are elsewhere.

For whatever else I have composed here besides liberation, that was done according to the conventions of poetry so that it might be as palatable as bitter medicine mixed with honey, thinking: "How might it become pleasing to the heart? (Saundarananda 18.63).

Having observed that the world for the most part is intent on the pleasure of sense-objects and averse to liberation, I have here explained the reality under the guise of poetry, [stating] that "liberation is supreme.

Having understood this, one should attentively grasp from this work that which pertains to tranquility, and not what is merely elegant; for gold, which is certainly beneficial, is extracted from the dust of ore.
The eighteenth canto, titled "The Declaration of the Command," in the epic poem *Saundarananda*.
This is the work of the venerable master Ācārya Aśvaghoṣa, a great poet and eminent disputant, a monk of Sāketa and a son of the noble Suvarṇākṣī.
